learningObjectives: Identify the inputs and assumptions for a two-sample sample size calculation.
Describe type I and type II errors without reversing conditional probabilities.
Apply prespecified confidence interval rules for superiority, noninferiority and equivalence.

keyConcepts.explanation: With a fixed sample and test, power depends on the true effect and variability. Smaller meaningful effects, greater SD or stricter alpha usually require more participants.

When higher is better, rule out an unacceptable loss by placing the lower confidence limit above the prespecified negative margin. An effective active control and a trial able to distinguish effective from ineffective treatment underpin interpretation.

Both bounds must lie within justified margins at the confidence level specified for the test. For two one-sided tests at 5% each, use the corresponding 90% two-sided interval. Here the stated rule uses a 95% interval.

In noninferiority trials, deviations and crossover can dilute differences. Check the prespecified estimand and supporting analysis sets, including per-protocol sensitivity analyses when appropriate. Agreement across analyses helps but cannot rescue poor trial conduct.

misconceptions.claim: Power of 90% means the treatment is 90% likely to work.
misconceptions.correction: It is the chance of rejecting a null under a specified true effect and model in repeated trials.

misconceptions.claim: A nonsignificant superiority test proves equivalence.
misconceptions.correction: It can leave worthwhile benefits or harms compatible with the data. Equivalence needs justified margins and an interval narrow enough to exclude both.

workedExample.design: Independent equal-sized arms and common SD for planning. A separate completed-trial example uses an approximate normal interval and a 2.5-point prechosen margin.
workedExample.interpretation: Plan for 133 analysable or 148 recruited participants per arm at 4 points. In the separate example, conclude noninferiority only if the margin, estimand, active-control evidence and conduct support that inference.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why does 133 describe each arm rather than the whole trial?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: The equal-arm power calculation reports n per group. Double that number for the analysable total.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Would a 95% interval of −1 to +1 establish superiority, noninferiority or equivalence under the stated rules?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: It crosses zero and satisfies both margin criteria. Whether those claims are justified also depends on the design and prespecified tests.

rProgression.menus: In Analysis → Sample Size → Unpaired t, set mean difference 4, SD 10, allocation 1:1, power 90% and alpha 5%.
rProgression.bridge: Compare the reported arm count with the rounded equal-variance R calculation.
rProgression.coding: Change SD, target effect and power one at a time. Revisit the chosen margin separately.

practiceQuestions.objective: Apply a loss allowance to a per-arm sample size.
practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional two-arm trial needs 108 analysable participants in each arm. Investigators expect 15% of recruited participants to have no primary outcome in each arm. Based on this allowance alone, what is the minimum integer recruitment target per arm?

options.feedback: This is the number needed for analysis and does not allow for loss.
Adding 15% of the analysable count underestimates loss, which is expected among those recruited.
This target leaves 107.1 expected analysable participants per arm.
Dividing 108 by 0.85 gives approximately 127.06, which rounds up to 128.
255 comes from rounding up the combined calculation 216/0.85. The target is per arm, so round up 108/0.85 separately for each arm.

practiceQuestions.hint: If N is recruited, the expected number available is 0.85 × N.
practiceQuestions.lesson: Inflate the analysable target by dividing by the fraction expected to remain.

lessons.title: Reading a clinical trial beyond its abstract
lessons.objective: Trace a trial from enrolment to analysis and judge whether its effect estimate answers the clinical question.
lessons.summary: A random sequence generates assignments. Allocation concealment keeps the next assignment unknown during enrolment. Blinding limits knowledge after allocation. For a treatment-policy comparison, follow participants in their assigned groups even after stopping treatment. An intention-to-treat label does not resolve unobserved outcomes. Compare the abstract against registration, protocol, participant flow and analysis. Check whether the endpoint matters directly to patients or is a surrogate.
lessons.challenge: An abstract says a new care pathway reduced relapses in treatment completers. Which three details would you request before advising a service to change practice?
lessons.steps: In a fictional parallel trial, 120 people are randomised per arm. Relapses occur in 18 of 100 observed people assigned the pathway and 24 of 114 observed controls. The observed risk difference is −3.1 percentage points. Assigning all missing pathway outcomes and no missing controls as events gives +11.7 points. Reversing the assignments gives −10.0 points. These are bounds based on extreme scenarios. Check missingness, assessor masking, endpoint and protocol. Weigh absolute effects, uncertainty, harms and applicability. Ward randomisation requires accounting for clustering. In crossover trials compare within people and assess period effects, washout and carryover.
lessons.r:
# Fictional relapse counts, following original group allocation
randomised <- c(pathway = 120, usual_care = 120)
observed <- c(pathway = 100, usual_care = 114)
events <- c(pathway = 18, usual_care = 24)
missing <- randomised - observed
rd <- function(risks) unname(risks[1] - risks[2])
observed_rd <- rd(events / observed)
favourable_rd <- rd((events + c(0, missing[2])) / randomised)
unfavourable_rd <- rd((events + c(missing[1], 0)) / randomised)
print(c(available_case_RD = observed_rd, best_for_pathway = favourable_rd,
        worst_for_pathway = unfavourable_rd))
stopifnot(abs(observed_rd - (18/100 - 24/114)) < 1e-12,
          abs(favourable_rd + 0.10) < 1e-12,
          abs(unfavourable_rd - 14/120) < 1e-12)

learningObjectives: Distinguish sequence generation, concealment and blinding.
Reconstruct the analysed denominators and identify deviations, missingness and selective reporting.
Recognise when allocation or measurement structure changes the unit of analysis.

keyConcepts.explanation: Protect enrolment from foreknowledge of the next assignment. Secure central allocation is one way. A computer-generated list alone cannot conceal assignments if recruiters can see it.
Document who knew the assignments and when. Masking outcome assessors can limit assessment bias even when patients and clinicians cannot be masked.

Define whose outcomes, the endpoint and time, the treatment contrast and how to handle events like stopping or switching therapy. State how missing outcomes are addressed and test sensitivity to assumptions.

How people feel, function or survive can be measured directly. A surrogate, such as a laboratory marker, stands in for a clinical outcome and needs evidence that intervention effects on the marker predict effects on that outcome in context. Prognostic association alone is insufficient.
People in the same randomised ward are likely correlated. Outcomes from different treatment periods in one person are paired. Carryover can confuse a crossover effect even with the correct pairing.

misconceptions.claim: Randomisation makes all later exclusions harmless.
misconceptions.correction: Exclusions and outcome loss after allocation can undermine comparability.

misconceptions.claim: Reporting CONSORT items establishes low risk of bias.
misconceptions.correction: Good reporting shows what was done and enables appraisal. It cannot replace sound conduct.

workedExample.design: Two equal groups with different amounts of missing follow-up. Event means relapse by a fixed endpoint. Status of those not observed is unknown.
workedExample.interpretation: The available-case estimate favours the pathway, but plausible concerns about missingness must be addressed before accepting a causal benefit. The extreme scenarios show why the abstract alone is insufficient.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Which protection is needed when an enrolment nurse can read the next listed treatment?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Conceal forthcoming allocations before enrolment is final.

teachingPrompts.prompt: The protocol specifies 12-week relapse, but the abstract promotes a 4-week laboratory marker instead. What would you ask?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Identify the prespecified outcome and time, check amendments and both outcomes, and consider selective reporting. Ask whether treatment-induced changes in this marker reliably predict changes in relapse in this setting.

rProgression.menus: Use the randomisation help to distinguish sequence generation and concealment.

rProgression.coding: Change event counts among the missing across a range of plausible scenarios and report when the sign changes.

practiceQuestions.objective: Identify the process that prevents selective enrolment.
practiceQuestions.stem: A trial compares two rehabilitation schedules. A computer creates the random allocation sequence, but the enrolment therapist can see the next assignment before confirming a patient's eligibility and consent. Which design change most directly addresses this weakness?

options.text: Ask participants not to tell the outcome assessor which schedule they receive.
options.feedback: This protects outcome assessment after assignment, leaving the recruitment problem.

options.text: Use more centres without changing enrolment.
options.feedback: The same foreknowledge can influence enrolment in any number of centres.

options.text: Make the allocation list available only to the enrolment therapist.
options.feedback: That therapist can still alter enrolment after seeing the assignment.

options.text: Adjust the results for recorded age and baseline severity.
options.feedback: Adjustment is not a substitute for preventing selective enrolment, including selection on unmeasured factors.

options.text: Use a secure service to reveal the next assignment only after eligibility and consent are recorded.
options.feedback: Correct. This conceals forthcoming assignments until enrolment is fixed.

practiceQuestions.hint: Ask what the recruiter can know before the participant is enrolled.
practiceQuestions.lesson: Allocation concealment occurs before assignment. Blinding refers to knowledge after assignment.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Recruiters who can see the next assignment can selectively enrol or delay patients. A secure service releasing it only after enrolment limits that opportunity.

lessons.title: Using likelihood ratios and evaluating diagnostic thresholds
lessons.objective: Update a pretest probability with a likelihood ratio and judge whether diagnostic study results apply to the patient.
lessons.summary: Bayes’ theorem updates pretest odds using the likelihood ratio for the result. The likelihood ratio compares how often that result occurs in people with and without the target condition. Multiply pretest odds by the ratio and convert back to probability. A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve displays sensitivity and the false-positive proportion across thresholds. Before applying an estimate, check the reference standard, who received it and whether the study patients resemble the intended population.
lessons.challenge: A test's sensitivity is reported as 95% in a sample of severe cases and healthy volunteers. What additional evidence would you need before using that estimate in a general practice population with uncertain diagnoses?
lessons.steps: Use fictional marker scores for people with (1, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) and without (0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5) the condition. Higher values suggest disease. At a positive threshold of at least 4, sensitivity and specificity are both 80%. LR+ = 0.80/0.20 = 4 and LR− = 0.20/0.80 = 0.25. With a separate, clinically justified pretest probability of 20%, odds are 1:4. A positive result raises probability to 50%, and a negative result lowers it to about 5.9%. At threshold 5, sensitivity drops to 60% and specificity rises to 90%. Plot the thresholds and connect these changes to the harms of missed diagnoses and unnecessary follow-up. The small sample teaches arithmetic. It cannot establish a reliable clinical threshold. In StatsDirect select one ROC series, then choose Condition present at the first column prompt and Condition absent at the next. Compare the AUC and use the R exercise to calculate likelihood ratios at a specified threshold.
lessons.r:
# Fictional independent test results, with known condition status
disease <- c(1,3,4,4,5,5,6,7,8,9)
no_disease <- c(0,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,5)
thresholds <- c(Inf, sort(unique(c(disease, no_disease)), decreasing = TRUE))
roc <- data.frame(threshold = thresholds,
  sensitivity = sapply(thresholds, function(t) mean(disease >= t)),
  specificity = sapply(thresholds, function(t) mean(no_disease < t)))
at4 <- subset(roc, threshold == 4)
at5 <- subset(roc, threshold == 5)
lr <- c(positive = at4$sensitivity / (1 - at4$specificity),
        negative = (1 - at4$sensitivity) / at4$specificity)
pretest_odds <- 0.20 / 0.80
posttest_odds <- lr * pretest_odds
posttest_probability <- posttest_odds / (1 + posttest_odds)
auc <- mean(outer(disease, no_disease, function(a, b) (a > b) + 0.5*(a == b)))
print(roc)
print(posttest_probability)
print(c(AUC = auc))
stopifnot(abs(lr[1] - 4) < 1e-12, abs(lr[2] - 0.25) < 1e-12,
          max(abs(posttest_probability - c(0.5, 1/17))) < 1e-12,
          at5$sensitivity == 0.6, at5$specificity == 0.9, abs(auc - 0.845) < 1e-12)

learningObjectives: Apply Bayes’ theorem in odds form to update a pretest probability.
Read ROC coordinates and interpret what AUC measures.
Recognise spectrum and verification problems and communicate uncertainty.

keyConcepts.explanation: Post-test odds = pretest odds × likelihood ratio. For a binary result, LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) and LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity. Use both parts of each ratio from the same threshold and relevant population.

keyConcepts.term: ROC and area under the curve (AUC)
keyConcepts.explanation: A point gives sensitivity against 1 − specificity. The empirical AUC here is 0.845, the probability of a randomly selected case score exceeding a randomly selected noncase score, counting ties as halves. It does not set the clinical threshold.
Severity, comorbidity and setting can change accuracy. If the reference diagnosis is obtained mainly in test-positive participants, estimates based only on those verified can be biased.

Describe the estimated chance in context, relate it to possible next steps and explain the limitations. For this illustration, about 50 of 100 similar people with a positive result would have the condition if the estimates apply.

misconceptions.claim: An LR of four means a 20% chance becomes 80%.
misconceptions.correction: The LR multiplies odds. Here a positive result moves 20% to 50%.

misconceptions.claim: A high AUC tells us which cut-off maximises patient benefit.
misconceptions.correction: AUC describes ranking across thresholds. Consequences of errors, prevalence, preferences and costs inform the chosen cut-off.

workedExample.design: Two equal-sized illustrative score groups with complete reference status. The 20% pretest estimate is supplied separately because the artificial 50:50 study case mix does not describe clinical prevalence.
workedExample.interpretation: A positive at threshold 4 gives 50% under the stated assumptions. A negative leaves residual risk. Describe that uncertainty without labelling either result diagnostic.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Would you say that a negative result rules the condition out?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: No. State the remaining probability and why the next step depends on the clinical context.

teachingPrompts.prompt: If the reference standard is applied mainly to those testing positive, which entries in the diagnostic table become uncertain?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Disease and nondisease status among unverified negative results are unknown. Complete-case sensitivity and specificity may be biased. The direction and size depend on the verification process.

rProgression.menus: Put the marked scores in separate condition-present and condition-absent columns and open Graphics → ROC.
rProgression.bridge: Match sensitivity and false-positive fractions to threshold points. Use the R calculation to update the odds at one point. The ROC example deliberately has equal numbers with and without the condition. Its predictive values reflect that artificial case mix. For the clinical scenario, start from the stated 20% pretest probability.
rProgression.coding: Change the pretest probability separately from the threshold and explain what each change affects.

practiceQuestions.objective: Convert a negative likelihood ratio to a remaining probability.
practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional test has sensitivity 75% and specificity 80% at a fixed threshold. A patient's pretest probability of the condition is 40%. Assuming these estimates apply to the patient, what is the approximate probability after a negative result?

options.feedback: 12.5% comes from multiplying the pretest probability by 0.3125. The likelihood ratio multiplies the pretest odds.
Correct. Prior odds 2/3 multiplied by 0.25/0.80 give 5/24. Convert to probability 5/29.
This is the proportion of people with the condition who test negative, not the chance of disease after a negative test.
31.3% expresses LR− = 0.3125 as a rounded percentage. Calculate post-test odds before converting back to probability.
68.8% expresses 1 − LR− = 0.6875 as a rounded percentage. Taking that complement does not update the pretest probability.

practiceQuestions.hint: Use the false-negative fraction divided by specificity, and multiply odds rather than probability.
practiceQuestions.lesson: A negative result lowers the odds when its LR is below 1. Convert the remaining odds to a probability before communicating it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The negative LR is 0.25/0.80 = 0.3125. Prior odds are 0.40/0.60 = 2/3. The updated probability is (5/24)/(1 + 5/24), or about 17.2%.

lessons.title: Evaluating a screening programme
lessons.objective: Judge screening on outcomes in the population offered it and compare benefits, harms and participation using appropriate denominators.
lessons.summary: A screening programme offers a pathway to an eligible population. Follow invitations, uptake, results, diagnosis and management through to outcomes. Counting additional diagnoses or comparing survival after diagnosis can exaggerate benefit. To estimate the effect of offering screening, compare outcomes by assigned invitation group where randomised evidence is available. Also measure harms, including false alarms, overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment. For antenatal screening, enabling an informed personal choice may itself be a programme goal.
lessons.challenge: A prenatal programme reports higher uptake and more detected cases. What additional outcomes, decisions and denominators do you need before deciding whether access and informed choice improved?
lessons.steps: In a fictional ten-year invitation trial, 40,000 people are assigned an invitation and 40,000 usual care. There are 80 and 100 deaths from the target condition. Compare all assigned people, giving 2.0 versus 2.5 deaths per 1,000 and a difference of −0.5 per 1,000. The point estimate is 20 fewer deaths per 40,000 invited. An approximate interval in R includes zero. Among 30,000 invited people who attend, 600 screen positive and all have known follow-up status. Of those, 120 have the target condition and 480 do not. The proportion of positive results confirmed is 120/600 = 20%. There were 480 false-positive results per 30,000 attendees, or 16 per 1,000. Check harms in both groups, including downstream procedures and overdiagnosis. These false-positive counts do not measure overdiagnosis.
lessons.r:
# Fictional trial, equal complete follow-up from random assignment
deaths <- c(invited = 80, usual_care = 100)
n <- c(invited = 40000, usual_care = 40000)
p <- deaths / n
rd <- unname(p[1] - p[2])
se <- sqrt(sum(p * (1 - p) / n))
ci <- rd + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
print(1000 * c(p, risk_difference = rd, lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2]))
positive <- 600
confirmed <- 120
attended <- 30000
ppv <- confirmed / positive
false_positive_per_1000 <- 1000 * (positive - confirmed) / attended
print(c(PPV = ppv, false_positive_per_1000 = false_positive_per_1000))
# Separate fictional maternity indicators for the same period and geography
live_births <- 40000
stillbirths <- 120
early_neonatal_deaths <- 40
maternal_deaths <- 3
maternal_ratio <- 1e5 * maternal_deaths / live_births
perinatal_rate <- 1000 * (stillbirths + early_neonatal_deaths) / (live_births + stillbirths)
print(c(maternal_per_100000_live_births = maternal_ratio,
        perinatal_per_1000_total_births = perinatal_rate))
stopifnot(abs(rd + .0005) < 1e-12, ci[1] < 0, ci[2] > 0, ppv == .2,
          false_positive_per_1000 == 16, maternal_ratio == 7.5,
          round(perinatal_rate, 2) == 3.99)

Explain informed choice and distinguish maternal and perinatal indicators.

keyConcepts.explanation: Earlier diagnosis adds time measured from diagnosis even when death occurs at the same time. Screening also preferentially finds conditions with a longer detectable preclinical phase. Both can improve observed survival from diagnosis without demonstrating that screening postpones death.

Overdiagnosis identifies real disease that would not have become symptomatic or caused harm in that person without screening. A false positive is an abnormal screening result when the target condition is absent.

Review whether eligible pregnant people can make an informed decision, understand a higher-chance result and access appropriate follow-up. Report offer, uptake, diagnostic follow-up and meaningful outcomes separately. There is no single desirable uptake rate that establishes informed choice.

The WHO maternal mortality ratio uses maternal deaths in the defined time window per 100,000 live births. The ONS perinatal mortality rate combines stillbirths and deaths under 7 days per 1,000 total births, using its defined birth and gestation criteria. Early neonatal mortality uses live births. Check place, period, gestational threshold and data completeness before comparing figures.

misconceptions.claim: Five-year survival after diagnosis rose, so screening saved lives.
misconceptions.correction: Diagnosis can occur earlier or preferentially find slowly progressing conditions. Compare outcomes from a common population starting point.

misconceptions.claim: Every unconfirmed positive result is an overdiagnosis.
misconceptions.correction: A false alarm has no target condition. An overdiagnosis is a real condition that would not cause harm in the absence of screening.

workedExample.design: Fictional random allocation to invitation or usual care, fixed ten-year follow-up and target-condition deaths. Harms and maternal indicators illustrate separate denominators.
workedExample.interpretation: The mortality difference is imprecise. Confirmed positives and false alarms describe the screening pathway, and the trade-off also needs harms and outcomes measured by invitation group.

teachingPrompts.prompt: If people die at the same age but receive a diagnosis two years earlier, what happens to survival from diagnosis?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: It increases by two years in this example even though life is not extended.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why is comparing attendees with nonattendees weaker than comparing invitation assignments?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Attendees may differ systematically in risk, access and other care. Analysing by assignment preserves randomisation and estimates the effect of offering the programme.

lessons.title: Time to event and competing risks
lessons.topic: Risk sets, competing events and survival comparisons
lessons.objective: Choose an event definition, time origin and estimator that match the question.
lessons.summary: Define the start of follow-up, event and censoring. A right-censored participant contributes observed time at risk. Kaplan–Meier multiplies conditional probabilities of remaining free of the specified event. Find the median from where the estimated curve reaches or drops below 0.50. If it stays above 0.50, the median has not been reached. Death before relapse prevents first relapse and enters its real-world cumulative incidence as a competing event. Log-rank compares curves using observed and expected event counts. A Cox hazard ratio describes relative instantaneous event rates. Its usual constant summary assumes proportional hazards.
lessons.challenge: After cancer treatment, how does death before relapse differ from ending observation at the last known relapse-free visit?
lessons.steps: In the fictional oncology data, use Analysis → Survival Analysis → Kaplan–Meier. Select Time (months), Composite event (1 = relapse or death before relapse, 0 = censored) and use Arm to identify the two groups. Usual care is Arm 0. Compare its composite event-free estimate at month 4 with R's 4/9. The curve first drops past 50% at month 4, so its median composite event-free time is four months. For relapse alone use the R calculation with Event type (0 = censored, 1 = relapse, 2 = death before relapse). It gives relapse cumulative incidence 7/18. Censoring deaths and taking 1 minus Kaplan–Meier instead gives 4/9. Both comparisons use a deliberately tiny dataset.
lessons.r:
# Fictional first-event oncology follow-up. 0=censored, 1=relapse, 2=death before relapse.
time <- c(1:6, seq(1.5,6.5))
kind <- c(1,2,0,1,2,0, 2,1,0,2,0,0)
arm <- rep(0:1,each=6)
any_event <- kind != 0
t <- time[arm==0]; k <- kind[arm==0]
et <- sort(t[k!=0])
n <- vapply(et,function(u) sum(t>=u),integer(1))
d1 <- vapply(et,function(u) sum(t==u & k==1),integer(1))
d2 <- vapply(et,function(u) sum(t==u & k==2),integer(1))
event_free <- cumprod(1-(d1+d2)/n)
before <- c(1,head(event_free,-1))
relapse <- cumsum(before*d1/n)
death <- cumsum(before*d2/n)
naive <- 1-cumprod(1-d1/n)
i <- match(4,et)
stopifnot(all.equal(event_free+relapse+death,rep(1,length(et))),
          abs(event_free[i]-4/9)<1e-12, abs(relapse[i]-7/18)<1e-12,
          abs(naive[i]-4/9)<1e-12)
print(data.frame(month=et, at_risk=n, event_free, relapse, death, naive))
# The step crosses 0.5 at an event in this example, with no plateau at 0.5.
stopifnot(event_free[i-1] > .5, event_free[i] < .5)
print(c(median_event_free_months = et[i]))
# Composite endpoint. This teaching partial likelihood has no ties.
events <- sort(time[any_event])
n0 <- vapply(events,function(u) sum(time>=u & arm==0),integer(1))
n1 <- vapply(events,function(u) sum(time>=u & arm==1),integer(1))
o1 <- sum(arm[any_event])
chi <- (o1-sum(n1/(n0+n1)))^2/sum(n0*n1/(n0+n1)^2)
p <- pchisq(chi,1,lower.tail=FALSE)
log_likelihood <- function(beta) beta*o1-sum(log(n0+n1*exp(beta)))
hr <- exp(optimize(log_likelihood,c(-10,10),maximum=TRUE)$maximum)
stopifnot(abs(chi-.2832613)<1e-6,abs(p-.5945716)<1e-6,abs(hr-.6670618)<1e-4)
print(c(logrank=chi,p_value=p,composite_HR=hr))
plot(c(0,et,6),c(0,relapse,tail(relapse,1)),type="s",ylim=c(0,1),
     xlab="Months after treatment",ylab="Cumulative incidence",main="Fictional usual-care cohort")
lines(c(0,et,6),c(0,death,tail(death,1)),type="s",lty=2)
legend("topleft",c("First relapse","Death before relapse"),lty=1:2,bty="n")

learningObjectives: Build risk sets immediately before event times.
Read a Kaplan–Meier curve and determine whether the median event-free time is estimable.
Distinguish composite event-free survival from cause-specific cumulative incidence.
Interpret log-rank and Cox results and recognise non-proportional hazards.

keyConcepts.explanation: The event has not been recorded by the last observed event-free time. Censoring removes a person from later risk sets without causing a Kaplan–Meier drop. Follow-up losses associated with prognosis can bias estimates.

Read the 0.50 crossing on the step curve for the defined event. When a step jumps across 0.50, use the event time. StatsDirect and R use the midpoint for a plateau exactly at 0.50 between successive event times. The last censored time alone does not give a median.
Sum observed versus expected events across risk sets. The test is especially sensitive under proportional hazards and can miss opposing early and late differences.
Compare instantaneous rates among those still at risk at the same time with specified covariates fixed. Inspect time patterns, such as scaled Schoenfeld residuals, before relying on a constant ratio.

Aalen–Johansen adds each cause's event increment weighted by the probability of remaining free of every first event just beforehand. A cause-specific hazard ratio alone does not determine cumulative incidence.

misconceptions.claim: A censoring mark is a failed outcome.
misconceptions.correction: It records the end of observation and alters subsequent risk sets.

misconceptions.claim: HR 0.67 means 33% fewer relapses by month six.
misconceptions.correction: The example HR concerns the composite instantaneous event rate. A risk ratio at six months answers a different question.

misconceptions.claim: Censor competing deaths to estimate the observed-world relapse risk with Kaplan–Meier.
misconceptions.correction: Use cumulative incidence for that probability. Removing deaths from risk sets in a cause-specific hazard model answers a hazard question.

workedExample.design: Twelve fictional oncology patients enter follow-up at the same clinical milestone. In usual care, two have first relapse, two die before relapse and two are right-censored. The two-group exercise uses the composite.
workedExample.interpretation: In usual care at month 4, relapse incidence is 7/18, death before relapse is 1/6 and composite event-free survival is 4/9. These estimates sum to one. The median time free of either event is four months. The small-sample log-rank P of about 0.59 and Cox HR of about 0.67 provide little information about efficacy or equivalence.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Who is at risk just before month 4 in usual care?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Three people remain observed and free of both first events.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why add (2/3) × (1/3) to relapse incidence at month 4?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Two-thirds are estimated free of both events before month 4, and one of the three then at risk relapses.

teachingPrompts.prompt: What if a treatment lowers both the relapse and early death hazards?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: The directions need not determine the real-world relapse probability. More patients may survive long enough to relapse. Inspect both cumulative incidences.

teachingPrompts.prompt: The last observation is censored at 12 months and the Kaplan–Meier curve is still above 50%. How would you report the median?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Report that the median was not reached during follow-up. The last censoring cannot replace the 50% crossing.

lessons.title: Choosing and interpreting regression models
lessons.objective: Choose a model for the outcome and explain what an adjusted coefficient means.
lessons.summary: Linear regression models a mean in the outcome's units, logistic regression models log odds for a binary outcome, and a Poisson model with a log exposure offset models a count rate. Adjust for selected covariates using the design and subject knowledge. Assess functional form, residuals, uncertainty and, for prediction, calibration beyond the development fit.
lessons.challenge: A new respiratory protocol is used more often for severe patients. How could a crude comparison obscure an association within levels of severity?
lessons.steps: Use Analysis → Regression and Correlation → Logistic with four fictional strata. Choose Grouped response data and include an intercept, with weighting off. Use Total as the number assessed, Events as the number who reattend, and Protocol and Severe as 0/1 predictors. The adjusted protocol odds ratio is 0.50, compared with about 0.85 when severity is omitted. Find the reference levels and interval. The R script also uses separate datasets for recovery days and counts accumulated over person-time. For the protocol odds ratio, base R gives a profile-likelihood 95% interval of about 0.331 to 0.748. It also shows the Wald interval (about 0.333 to 0.751) for comparison. Compare methods as well as endpoints.
lessons.r:
# Fictional respiratory service examples. Each model has its own outcome.
g <- data.frame(protocol=c(0,0,1,1),severe=c(0,1,0,1),total=c(200,100,90,210),events=c(40,50,10,70))
logistic <- glm(cbind(events,total-events)~protocol+severe,binomial(),g)
crude <- glm(cbind(events,total-events)~protocol,binomial(),g)
lr <- coef(logistic)["protocol"]
wald <- exp(lr+c(-1,1)*qnorm(.975)*sqrt(vcov(logistic)["protocol","protocol"]))
stopifnot(abs(exp(lr)-.5)<1e-8,abs(exp(coef(crude)["protocol"])-(80/220)/(90/210))<1e-8)
print(c(adjusted_OR=unname(exp(lr)),crude_OR=unname(exp(coef(crude)["protocol"])),Wald_lower=wald[1],Wald_upper=wald[2]))
no <- predict(logistic,transform(g,protocol=0),type="response")
yes <- predict(logistic,transform(g,protocol=1),type="response")
profile <- exp(confint(logistic, parm="protocol"))
stopifnot(all(abs(profile-c(.3312941,.7478764))<1e-6))
print(profile)
rd <- weighted.mean(yes-no,g$total)
stopifnot(abs(rd-((1/9-1/5)*290+(1/3-1/2)*310)/600)<1e-8)
print(c(standardised_probability_difference=rd))
days <- data.frame(protocol=rep(g$protocol,each=2),severe=rep(g$severe,each=2),days=c(5,7,9,11,3,5,7,9))
linear <- lm(days~protocol+severe,days)
stopifnot(abs(coef(linear)["protocol"]+2)<1e-10)
print(coef(summary(linear)))
rates <- transform(g,episodes=c(10,18,8,18),person_months=c(200,120,240,180))
rate <- glm(episodes~protocol+severe+offset(log(person_months)),poisson(),rates)
stopifnot(abs(exp(coef(rate)["protocol"])-2/3)<1e-8)
print(exp(coef(rate)))
# Fixed probabilities evaluated in a separate fictional population.
pred <- c(.2,.5,.8); n <- c(100,100,100); observed <- c(15,40,70)
stopifnot(abs(sum(observed)/sum(n)-125/300)<1e-12,weighted.mean(pred,n)==.5)
print(data.frame(predicted=pred,observed=observed/n))
plot(pred,observed/n,xlim=c(0,1),ylim=c(0,1),pch=19,
     xlab="Predicted probability",ylab="Observed proportion",main="Fictional model validation")
abline(0,1,lty=2)

learningObjectives: Match continuous, binary and count outcomes to the model and estimand.
Interpret adjusted differences, odds ratios and rate ratios.

keyConcepts.explanation: Choose adjustment variables using the study design and causal knowledge. Crude and conditional odds ratios sometimes differ even without confounding because odds ratios are noncollapsible.
A contrast can vary across severity levels. Include an interaction if justified and report contrasts for relevant groups. Interaction depends on the scale.
In log-rate regression, the coefficient of log exposure is fixed at one. The same rate over twice the exposure predicts twice the count.

Inspect residuals and variance in linear regression, functional form and separation in logistic regression, and dispersion and clustering in Poisson models. For prediction, check calibration and discrimination in appropriate evaluation data.

misconceptions.claim: OR 0.50 always halves the probability.

misconceptions.claim: Use log person-time as a freely estimated term for a rate ratio.
misconceptions.correction: Use a log offset to fix proportionality to exposure.

misconceptions.claim: A significant coefficient or high AUC proves calibration.
misconceptions.correction: Compare predicted probabilities with observed frequencies.

teachingPrompts.prompt: In the severe group, what risks go with OR 0.50?

teachingPrompts.prompt: What if protocol interacts with severity?

lessons.title: Do two measurements agree?
lessons.topic: Bland–Altman limits, kappa and intraclass correlation
lessons.objective: Choose an agreement measure for the scale, and decide what size of disagreement matters clinically.
lessons.summary: Correlation measures association. Two devices can rank patients almost identically and still give differences large enough to change care. For paired quantitative measures, inspect differences against their means and compare the limits of agreement with a prespecified acceptable range. For two categorical raters report the agreement table and observed agreement alongside Cohen's kappa. For quantitative reliability specify the ICC design, single or average rating, and whether absolute agreement or consistency matters.
lessons.challenge: Two paediatric respiratory devices have near-perfect correlation. What else would you need before replacing one with the other?
lessons.steps: In the fictional data, enter Reference reading and New reading from the same eight children. Select Analysis → Parametric → Paired t and request agreement analysis. With Reference selected first, StatsDirect uses Reference minus New: a mean of −2.5 units and limits around −4.84 and −0.16 units. The R script uses New minus Reference. Mean difference is +2.5 units and the usual 95% limits are about +0.16 and +4.84 units. The upper limit exceeds the example's prespecified ±3 tolerance. The separate R examples use a classification table for Cohen's kappa and an ANOVA decomposition for two single-measure ICCs. The illustrative sample is too small for an interchangeability decision.
lessons.r:
# One fictional pair per child, on the same measurement scale.
reference <- c(19,26,31,38,43,51,57,64)
new <- c(20,28,34,40,47,52,60,68)
mid <- (new+reference)/2
difference <- new-reference
bias <- mean(difference)
loa <- bias+c(-1,1)*1.96*sd(difference)
stopifnot(bias==2.5,all(abs(loa-c(.1573519,4.8426481))<1e-6),cor(reference,new)>.99)
print(c(correlation=cor(reference,new),bias=bias,lower=loa[1],upper=loa[2]))
plot(mid,difference,pch=19,ylim=range(c(difference,loa,-3,3)),
     xlab="Pair mean",ylab="New minus reference",main="Fictional device agreement")
abline(h=bias)
abline(h=loa,lty=2)
abline(h=c(-3,3),lty=3)
legend("bottomright",c("Mean difference","Limits of agreement","Clinical tolerance"),lty=1:3,bty="n")

# Separate nominal ratings from 100 fictional encounters.
ratings <- matrix(c(36,4,8,52),2,byrow=TRUE)
p_observed <- sum(diag(ratings))/sum(ratings)
p_expected <- sum(rowSums(ratings)*colSums(ratings))/sum(ratings)^2
kappa <- (p_observed-p_expected)/(1-p_expected)
stopifnot(p_observed==.88,abs(p_expected-.512)<1e-12,abs(kappa-(.88-.512)/(1-.512))<1e-12)
print(c(observed_agreement=p_observed,expected_agreement=p_expected,kappa=kappa))

# Balanced two-way ANOVA, one reading per device for each child.
y <- cbind(reference,new)
n <- nrow(y); k <- ncol(y); grand <- mean(y)
ms_subject <- k*sum((rowMeans(y)-grand)^2)/(n-1)
ms_device <- n*sum((colMeans(y)-grand)^2)/(k-1)
residual <- sweep(sweep(y,1,rowMeans(y)),2,colMeans(y))+grand
ms_error <- sum(residual^2)/((n-1)*(k-1))
icc_a <- (ms_subject-ms_error)/(ms_subject+(k-1)*ms_error+k*(ms_device-ms_error)/n)
icc_c <- (ms_subject-ms_error)/(ms_subject+(k-1)*ms_error)
stopifnot(abs(icc_a-.9854217)<1e-6,abs(icc_c-.9971900)<1e-6,icc_a<icc_c)
print(c(ICC_absolute_single=icc_a,ICC_consistency_single=icc_c))

learningObjectives: Distinguish association, agreement and reliability.
Estimate systematic difference and limits of agreement in the measurement's units.
Interpret a kappa alongside its agreement table and choose an appropriate ICC.

keyConcepts.explanation: Mean difference ± 1.96 SD estimates an interval containing about 95% of individual differences when the differences are approximately normal and their spread is stable. Confidence intervals around the limits quantify uncertainty in their estimates.

Look for proportional bias, changing spread and unusual pairs. Repeated measurements per person need analyses that account for their dependence. A clinically acceptable difference should be decided independently of the observed limits.

Compare observed agreement with agreement expected from the marginal category frequencies under independent classification. Kappa changes with category mix even at similar observed agreement. Show counts, agreement and uncertainty.

Quantifies the proportion of variability attributable to differences among subjects under a specified model. Use consistency for ranking and absolute agreement when the values must match. Name one-way or two-way model, fixed or random raters as appropriate, single or average measurement and confidence interval. A broad subject range can produce a high ICC despite important differences in units.

misconceptions.claim: A high correlation means interchangeable devices.
misconceptions.correction: A shift in every value can leave correlation unchanged. Compare paired differences with a clinical tolerance.

misconceptions.claim: The limits are a 95% confidence interval for bias.
misconceptions.correction: That interval concerns uncertainty in the mean difference. The limits describe the spread of individual differences.

misconceptions.claim: A high ICC removes the need to check absolute differences.
misconceptions.correction: Inspect the measurement-unit differences and context. ICC depends on how heterogeneous the subjects are.

workedExample.design: Eight fictional independent children, one measurement by each device, both taken at the same visit. A separate two-rater categorical dataset supplies the agreement table.
workedExample.interpretation: Correlation ≈ 0.998 and even the absolute-agreement single-measure ICC ≈ 0.985 are high in these widely dispersed measurements. The upper agreement limit still exceeds the example tolerance. In the categorical example, 88 of 100 ratings agree and unweighted kappa is approximately 0.75.

teachingPrompts.prompt: If every new reading exceeds its paired reference by five units, what happens to correlation?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: An additive shift does not lower correlation. The shift can still be clinically important.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why compare agreement limits with ±3 units?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: The acceptable difference depends on clinical decisions. The estimated limits show how far individual comparisons may differ.

practiceQuestions.objective: Compare individual differences with a tolerance.
practiceQuestions.stem: A new paediatric monitor correlates 0.99 with the existing one. For new minus existing, mean bias is +2.5 units and estimated limits of agreement are +0.16 to +4.84. Differences above 3 units in either direction matter clinically. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Correlation establishes interchangeability.
options.feedback: Ranking can agree even when paired differences are large.

options.text: The estimated upper limit exceeds the tolerance. Assess uncertainty before deciding on replacement.
options.feedback: The point estimate exceeds +3 and the estimates have sampling uncertainty.

options.text: A mean bias below 3 implies all individual differences are acceptable.
options.feedback: Mean bias summarises the average, rather than individual spread.

options.text: The two limits are the confidence interval for mean bias.
options.feedback: Limits of agreement describe individual differences.

options.text: Subtract the mean bias and declare all future readings safe.
options.feedback: A correction may reduce systematic bias, but residual spread and validation still matter.

practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the limit estimates with the prespecified range.
practiceQuestions.lesson: Correlation measures association. Two devices can rank patients almost identically and still give differences large enough to change care. For paired quantitative measures, inspect differences against their means and compare the limits of agreement with a prespecified acceptable range. For two categorical raters report the agreement table and observed agreement alongside Cohen's kappa. For quantitative reliability specify the ICC design, single or average rating, and whether absolute agreement or consistency matters.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The limit at +4.84 exceeds +3. Review its uncertainty and the clinical consequences. High correlation and an average difference below 3 are insufficient evidence for replacing the device.

lessons.title: Audit and monitoring improvement over time
lessons.topic: Clinical standards, control charts and case mix
lessons.objective: Choose a measure and chart for the service question, then respond appropriately to observed variation.
lessons.summary: An audit defines a standard, eligibility and a denominator, checks current care, acts on findings and remeasures. Quality improvement measures are followed in time order with a stable definition. A control chart estimates expected variation in a stable process. A p-chart models the proportion of eligible encounters with a binary outcome and its limits vary with denominator. Clinical targets, control limits and confidence intervals serve different purposes.
lessons.challenge: Two emergency department months each have 15% delayed reviews. One month has 100 eligible encounters and the other has 300. Could their statistical signals differ?
lessons.steps: In this fictional emergency department audit, the adverse outcome is a first clinical review recorded more than 60 minutes after arrival among eligible encounters with known review times. Review exclusions and quantify missing timestamps before comparing months. Enter the 14 chronological counts and eligible totals or run the supplied R script. Use only months 1–12 as the illustrative baseline and hold its 8% centre fixed. Under the simple binomial model the 3 SD upper limit is about 16.1% at n=100 and 12.7% at n=300. Both later months are at 15%, but only the larger month breaches its limit. Plot a separate 5% example service target. StatsDirect Graphics → Control illustrates fixed bands for a continuous series; use this R exercise for changing binomial limits.
lessons.r:
# Fictional ED audit. A patient encounter contributes at most one delayed review.
month <- 1:14
eligible <- c(100,125,150,100,175,125,100,150,125,175,100,175,100,300)
delayed <- c(7,11,11,10,12,9,9,13,10,14,7,15,15,45)
baseline <- 1:12
p0 <- sum(delayed[baseline])/sum(eligible[baseline])
observed <- delayed/eligible
band <- 3*sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/eligible)
lcl <- pmax(0,p0-band); ucl <- pmin(1,p0+band)
signal <- observed>ucl | observed<lcl
stopifnot(abs(p0-.08)<1e-12,all(abs(observed[13:14]-.15)<1e-12),
          identical(which(signal),14L),ucl[13]>.15,ucl[14]<.15)
print(data.frame(month,eligible,delayed,observed,lcl,ucl,signal))
plot(month,observed,type="o",ylim=c(0,max(ucl,observed)),pch=19,
     xlab="Month",ylab="Delayed review proportion",main="Fictional ED p-chart")
abline(h=p0,lty=2)
abline(h=.05,lty=3)
lines(month,lcl,lty=4); lines(month,ucl,lty=4)
abline(v=12.5,lty=2,col="grey50")
points(month[signal],observed[signal],pch=19,col="red")
legend("bottomleft",c("Baseline centre","Service target","Control limits"),lty=2:4,bty="n")

# Separate example: episodes during person-time, by frailty stratum.
# Rows are sites and columns are low/high frailty. All rates per 1,000 days.
cases <- rbind(A=c(1,18),B=c(8,8))
days <- rbind(A=c(1000,3000),B=c(4000,1000))
crude <- 1000*rowSums(cases)/rowSums(days)
standard <- drop(1000*(cases/days)%*%c(.5,.5))
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(crude),c(4.75,3.2)),
          all.equal(unname(standard),c(3.5,5)),crude[1]>crude[2],standard[1]<standard[2])
print(cbind(crude,standardised=standard))

learningObjectives: Define a reproducible process measure, denominator and audit standard.
Interpret changing p-chart limits under an explicit baseline.
Distinguish within-process variation, a clinical target and uncertainty about a rate.
Recognise case-mix effects and choose a constructive response to variation.

keyConcepts.explanation: Predefine eligibility, outcome, target and data source. Report missingness, compare performance with the standard, investigate causes, act and repeat. Monitor balancing measures such as review quality or staff burden.
With stable risk p and independent observations, limits are p ± 3√[p(1−p)/n], bounded by 0 and 1. Small counts, clustering or extra variability can require another method.

Check an unusual point against data quality, eligibility and local process changes before acting. Stable but inadequate performance calls for process redesign; repeatedly reacting to ordinary fluctuations can worsen variation. Annotate and revise the centre after evidence of a sustained change.

Control limits describe expected variation of subgroup proportions under a stable baseline. Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty in an estimated parameter. The service target expresses the desired performance.

Compare strata and apply common standardisation weights when useful. An adjusted rate depends on the target mix and measured variables. Different ascertainment, missingness or sparse counts still matter. A stable chart does not prove that adjustment is adequate.

misconceptions.claim: A point beyond the control limit proves an intervention worked.
misconceptions.correction: It is a reason to investigate. Data definition, case mix, staffing and chance remain possible explanations.

misconceptions.claim: All monthly percentages have the same precision.
misconceptions.correction: With different denominators their expected variability can differ markedly.

misconceptions.claim: A point within its control limits meets the performance standard.
misconceptions.correction: The target can lie well below a stable but inadequate process.

misconceptions.claim: A 95% confidence interval can replace a 3 SD control line.
misconceptions.correction: The interval and control line answer different questions.

workedExample.design: Twelve illustrative baseline months and two monitoring months. The two later proportions share a point estimate but have different denominators. A separate fictional comparison uses frailty-specific person-time rates at two sites.
workedExample.interpretation: Month 13 lies within the illustrative baseline limits and month 14 exceeds them. Check data quality and identify what led to the signal. Both miss the example target of at most 5%. The separate two-site example reverses the crude ordering after both sites receive the same case-mix weights. Confirm comparability and quantify uncertainty before treating it as a performance ranking.

teachingPrompts.prompt: How should the team respond to the month 14 point?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Check data completeness and changes in case mix and workflow. Investigate a possible special cause before crediting or blaming a change.

n <- c(500, 500)

                           c(.04,.02,.60,25,50,.01))))

learningObjectives: Translate a study's relative effects into absolute benefit and harm over a stated time.

keyConcepts.explanation: Subtract risks with the same follow-up. Keep the direction and units clear. A reduction from 10% to 6% is 4 percentage points, or a relative reduction of 40%.

keyConcepts.term: Number needed to treat or harm
keyConcepts.explanation: Use the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction or increase for the specified outcome and duration. Here the reciprocals are integers. Keep confidence intervals and competing outcomes in view.
If the risk ratio were stable across settings, a lower untreated risk would imply less absolute benefit. That assumption and the harm rate both need evidence.

misconceptions.claim: A 40% relative reduction prevents 40 admissions per 100 patients.
misconceptions.correction: Here the estimate is 4 fewer admissions per 100. Start from the control risk.

misconceptions.claim: Net benefit is NNH minus NNT.
misconceptions.correction: The two outcomes differ in importance; the same person can experience both. Consider severity, uncertainty and preferences.

lessons.title: Causal comparisons and effect modification
lessons.objective: Define a target comparison and distinguish confounding, mediation, selection and effect modification.
lessons.summary: Begin by imagining the trial you would run. Define eligibility, follow-up, the treatment strategies and the outcome. Then use a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to state which variables you assume cause others. Arrows point from cause to effect, and following them cannot bring you back to the same variable.
lessons.challenge: Which variables would you adjust for to estimate the total effect, and why? Explain what would make the adjusted result misleading.
lessons.steps: Draw the proposed DAG for the fictional cohort. A is age, T is treatment, Y is later admission, M is early improvement, F is a follow-up visit, and U is access to care. Draw A → T, A → Y, T → Y, T → M, M → Y, T → F, U → F and U → Y. Before checking the worked answer, mark the arrows that form an alternative path between treatment and admission. Choose which measured variable to adjust for. Then calculate the age-specific contrasts and use the same age weights for each treatment group.
lessons.r:
risk_t <- c(3/60, 24/160)
risk_c <- c(16/160, 18/60)
w <- c(.5,.5)
std_t <- sum(w*risk_t)
std_c <- sum(w*risk_c)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c(std_t,std_c,risk_t-risk_c,risk_t/risk_c),c(.10,.20,-.05,-.15,.5,.5))))
print(rbind(risk_ratio=risk_t/risk_c,risk_difference=risk_t-risk_c))
print(c(crude_t=27/220,crude_c=34/220,adjusted_t=std_t,adjusted_c=std_c))

learningObjectives: Define a target comparison and distinguish confounding, mediation, selection and effect modification.
Which variables would you adjust for to estimate the total effect, and why? Explain what would make the adjusted result misleading.

keyConcepts.explanation: Measured covariates must suffice to make treatment groups comparable, each strategy must occur for the people being compared, and observed outcomes must correspond to the strategies as defined. Also consider measurement, follow-up and interference.

A pre-treatment common cause of treatment and outcome can confound. A post-treatment intermediate can transmit part of the effect. Conditioning on a common effect of treatment and another cause of outcome can introduce bias.

A → T and A → Y create the backdoor path T ← A → Y. M carries part of the treatment effect. F is a collider on T → F ← U → Y. Restricting to patients who return for follow-up can open this path even when access to care does not determine treatment.
Differences in effect depend on the scale. A constant ratio can produce very different absolute benefits in populations with different baseline risks.

Standardisation averages risks over a target population. Propensity weighting uses the probability of receiving observed treatment given measured baseline covariates. Look for poor overlap, extreme weights and imbalance. An adjusted estimate still depends on design and assumptions.
Misaligning eligibility, treatment assignment and follow-up can give a group event-free time it had to survive to enter. A larger regression model alone does not fix this.

misconceptions.claim: Adjust for everything measured.
misconceptions.correction: Pick variables using the causal question and time ordering. Adjusting for intermediates or colliders can bias a total-effect estimate.

misconceptions.claim: No interaction on the relative scale means equal absolute benefit.
misconceptions.correction: That conclusion does not follow when untreated risks differ.

workedExample.design: Fictional pneumonia service cohort. Younger patients have 3/60 admissions on treatment and 16/160 untreated. Older patients have 24/160 on treatment and 18/60 untreated. Age is measured before treatment. Standardise to equal proportions of younger and older people.
workedExample.interpretation: For the total effect under the stated DAG, adjust for age to close T ← A → Y. Leave early improvement unadjusted so the mediated effect stays in the comparison. Do not select only follow-up attendees, since F is a collider. Standardising to the same 50:50 age mix gives 10% treated and 20% untreated. The risk difference is −10 points. Each age-specific risk ratio is 0.5, while the risk differences are −5 and −15 points. The graph and estimates still rely on stated assumptions.

lessons.title: Systematic reviews and certainty of evidence
lessons.objective: Read pooled effects, heterogeneity and prediction intervals alongside the certainty of the evidence.
lessons.summary: A systematic review follows a reproducible search and appraisal process. Pool studies only if their questions and effect measures can be sensibly combined. A forest plot shows individual study estimates and intervals alongside a pooled estimate when one is calculated.
lessons.challenge: An average effect favours the intervention but the prediction interval includes harm. How would you describe this to a service deciding whether to adopt it?
lessons.steps: Run the R example and read the forest plot for five fictional studies. Negative differences mean faster recovery with the intervention. Find the vertical null line at zero, then identify the first study's square and horizontal confidence interval. Compare the pooled diamond with the dashed prediction interval. Ask what might differ in a new setting and whether any studies share participants or comparator groups.
lessons.r:
y <- -4:0
v <- rep(1, length(y))
k <- length(y)
w <- 1/v
Q <- sum(w*(y-weighted.mean(y,w))^2)
i2 <- max(0,(Q-(k-1))/Q)
# Closed form of REML here because all within-study variances are equal.
tau2 <- max(0,var(y)-v[1])
wr <- 1/(v+tau2)
estimate <- weighted.mean(y,wr)
# HKSJ t interval and an approximate prediction interval (Cochrane handbook).
hk_se <- sqrt(sum(wr*(y-estimate)^2)/(k-1)/sum(wr))
ci <- estimate+c(-1,1)*qt(.975,k-1)*hk_se
pi <- estimate+c(-1,1)*qt(.975,k-1)*sqrt(tau2+hk_se^2)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c(Q,i2,tau2,estimate),c(10,.6,1.5,-2))),
          all(abs(ci-c(-3.96324,-.03676))<.0001),
          all(abs(pi-c(-5.92649,1.92649))<.0001))
print(round(c(Q=Q,I2=i2,tau2=tau2,mean_effect=estimate,CI=ci,PI=pi),3))
row <- k:1
lim <- qnorm(.975)*sqrt(v)
plot(y,row,xlim=range(y-lim,y+lim,pi),ylim=c(-1.5,k+.5),
     yaxt="n",ylab="",xlab="Difference in recovery time (days)",
     main="Forest plot: fictional recovery-time studies",pch=15)
axis(2,at=c(-1,0,row),labels=c("Prediction","Average",paste("Study",seq_len(k))),las=1)
abline(v=0,lty=2)
segments(y-lim,row,y+lim,row)
polygon(c(ci[1],estimate,ci[2],estimate),c(0,.25,0,-.25),col="grey30")
segments(pi[1],-1,pi[2],-1,lwd=2,lty=3)

learningObjectives: Read pooled effects, heterogeneity and prediction intervals alongside the certainty of the evidence.
An average effect favours the intervention but the prediction interval includes harm. How would you describe this to a service deciding whether to adopt it?

keyConcepts.explanation: A square shows a study estimate and its horizontal line shows a confidence interval. Square area can encode study weight. Here weights are equal. The centre of the diamond is the pooled estimate and its width is the pooled confidence interval. The separate dashed line shows the prediction interval.

Tau-squared estimates variance of underlying study effects on the analysis scale. I-squared estimates the share of observed variability attributed to heterogeneity rather than sampling error under the model; it is not the percentage of inconsistent studies.

A confidence interval for the average effect concerns uncertainty about that mean. A prediction interval adds heterogeneity to describe the plausible true effect in a comparable new setting. Both depend on model assumptions and can be unstable with few studies.

Funnel asymmetry can reflect selective reporting, genuine differences, chance or methodological differences between smaller and larger studies. Visual and formal checks have limited power with few studies.
Ask about risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. A very precise pooled estimate can still have low certainty.

Use a mean difference for the same scale, a standardised mean difference for compatible constructs measured on different scales, and a log scale for ratios. Avoid double counting shared controls or cohorts.

Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) helps readers see what the reviewers searched, screened, excluded and included. A clear report allows appraisal. It cannot by itself establish low risk of bias or high certainty.

misconceptions.claim: Use a fixed-effect model whenever the heterogeneity P value is above 0.05.
misconceptions.correction: A test can miss real heterogeneity with few studies. Choose the model based on the question, design and clinical diversity before seeing the results.

misconceptions.claim: A random-effects model solves information bias and makes any studies poolable.
misconceptions.correction: It models variation in true effects; it does not correct bias, non-comparable designs or dependent observations.

workedExample.design: Fictional five-study synthesis of an intervention's effect on recovery time. Differences are intervention minus usual care in days. Studies are independent. All have a reported SE of 1 day. Effects are −4, −3, −2, −1 and 0 days.
workedExample.interpretation: The estimated average is −2 days. In this teaching calculation the mean-effect 95% interval is about −3.96 to −0.04 days and the prediction interval is about −5.93 to +1.93 days. An average reduction allows benefits or increases at individual sites. This small example cannot validate the model.

practiceQuestions.objective: Distinguish the interval for a mean effect from an interval for a new setting.
practiceQuestions.stem: A meta-analysis estimates a 2-day average reduction in recovery time. Its 95% confidence interval for the mean excludes zero, but its prediction interval includes no reduction and some prolongation. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Every setting should expect a shorter recovery.
options.feedback: A confidence interval for a mean does not describe every setting.

options.text: The study outcomes must have been measured incorrectly.
options.feedback: The pattern can arise from real heterogeneity.

options.text: The two results contradict each other.
options.feedback: They are intervals for different quantities.

options.text: The result rules out increased recovery time in a new setting.
options.feedback: The prediction interval allows such an effect.

options.text: The estimated average favours the intervention, but effects in comparable settings may differ.
options.feedback: The distinction matters when choosing whether to adopt the intervention.

practiceQuestions.hint: Ask what each interval is intended to cover.
practiceQuestions.lesson: A pooled effect is a summary of study evidence, not a guaranteed local effect.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The mean-effect interval reflects uncertainty in the average. A prediction interval accounts for heterogeneity and allows no benefit or harm in a comparable setting under the model.

lessons.title: Population impact and health economic measures
lessons.objective: Distinguish individual risk, attributable burden, vaccine effectiveness and health economic comparisons.
lessons.summary: Give the target population, period and counterfactual. Group risk comparisons do not by themselves establish the outcomes that would change if an exposure or programme changed.
lessons.challenge: Explain the difference between the observed burden, the burden possibly avoidable under an intervention, and whether the intervention is affordable.
lessons.steps: Calculate a population risk difference and attributable fraction under the stated assumptions. Then compare the extra cost and extra quality-adjusted life years of two fictional strategies.
lessons.r:
pop <- c(1000,4000)
events <- c(100,200)
obs <- sum(events)/sum(pop)
scenario <- .05
paf <- (obs-scenario)/obs
icer <- 50000/2
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c(obs,sum(pop)*(obs-scenario),paf,icer),c(.06,50,1/6,25000))))
print(c(observed=obs,counterfactual=scenario,population_fraction=paf,extra_cost_per_QALY=icer))

learningObjectives: Distinguish individual risk, attributable burden, vaccine effectiveness and health economic comparisons.
Explain the difference between the observed burden, the burden possibly avoidable under an intervention, and whether the intervention is affordable.

keyConcepts.explanation: Compare the observed population risk with the risk under a specified intervention, divided by the observed risk. Using the unexposed risk for everyone requires strong causal and transport assumptions.

For a comparable risk comparison, 1 minus the risk ratio estimates relative risk reduction. Interpret relative to the outcome, follow-up and vaccination strategy. In observational data consider confounding, prior infection, selection and ascertainment.

Check the definitions and denominators of maternal, neonatal and perinatal measures. The standardised mortality ratio divides observed by expected events based on reference rates; state whether reported as a ratio or as a percentage.

A QALY combines time and health utility. A DALY represents years of life lost plus years lived with disability. Years of potential life lost uses a stated age reference; these measures answer different questions.

Divide the difference in costs by the difference in health benefits for the relevant comparator. Specify the perspective, horizon, discounting and uncertainty. Cost effectiveness does not establish affordability.

misconceptions.claim: A risk ratio of 2 means half of all cases in the population are attributable.
misconceptions.correction: Population impact depends on exposure distribution and the counterfactual risk.

misconceptions.claim: Compare each programme's cost divided by its own total QALYs.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the extra costs to the extra benefits relative to the alternative.

workedExample.design: Fictional cohort: 1,000 exposed residents have 100 events; 4,000 unexposed have 200 events during the same year. If an intervention reduced exposed risk to 5% without other changes, the population would have 250 instead of 300 events. Separately, a new programme costs 50,000 more and produces 2 more QALYs in this exercise.
workedExample.interpretation: Under the stated scenario the population risk changes from 6% to 5%: a relative reduction in population events of 50/300, about 16.7%. The crude exposed vs unexposed risk ratio is 2. The incremental programme cost is 25,000 per additional QALY.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between the observed burden, the burden possibly avoidable under an intervention, and whether the intervention is affordable.
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: State the assumptions behind assigning everyone a 5% risk. Do not multiply a relative reduction by all events. Keep a separate budget and sensitivity analysis for the programme.

rProgression.menus: Tabulate people and events per group. Use a two-group risk comparison for the observed cohort.
rProgression.bridge: In R compute the absolute and relative differences under an explicit hypothetical change.
rProgression.coding: Vary exposure prevalence and the counterfactual risk; then vary programme cost and benefits independently.

practiceQuestions.objective: Calculate a population attributable fraction from a stated scenario.
practiceQuestions.stem: A population has 300 annual cases. A defined intervention is expected to prevent 50 of them without other changes. What proportion of the current population cases would it prevent?

options.feedback: This might be a change in population risk if population size were known, not the proportion of current cases.
This is not the ratio of prevented to observed cases.
Fifty divided by 300 is one sixth.
The numerator is a count of 50 cases.
This is the fraction of cases expected to remain.

practiceQuestions.hint: Use the total number of current cases as the denominator.
practiceQuestions.lesson: Keep population risk and fraction of cases distinct.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Under the assumptions the intervention would avert 50/300, or about 16.7% of current cases.

lessons.title: Uncertainty, multiplicity and sensitivity analyses
lessons.objective: Assess how missing outcomes, multiple comparisons and alternative assumptions can change an analysis.
lessons.summary: Separate sampling error from bias and reporting choices. Be explicit about which questions are confirmatory. Show how conclusions change under plausible assumptions about data you cannot observe.
lessons.challenge: Describe why neither a P value nor a narrower confidence interval can resolve uncertainty about missing outcomes. Suggest a sensitivity analysis and a plan for primary and exploratory outcomes.
lessons.steps: Compute the probability of at least one false positive across 20 independent true nulls tested at 0.05. Then compute outcome bounds with missing follow-up in a randomised study.
lessons.r:
fwer <- 1-(1-.05)^20
sample_n <- c(100,100)
observed <- c(8,12)
missing <- c(10,10)
low <- observed/sample_n
high <- (observed+missing)/sample_n
rd_bound <- c(low[1]-high[2],high[1]-low[2])
stopifnot(abs(fwer-.6415141)<1e-7,isTRUE(all.equal(rd_bound,c(-.14,.06))))
print(c(FWER=fwer,Bonferroni_cutoff=.05/20,min_RD=rd_bound[1],max_RD=rd_bound[2]))

learningObjectives: Assess how missing outcomes, multiple comparisons and alternative assumptions can change an analysis.
Describe why neither a P value nor a narrower confidence interval can resolve uncertainty about missing outcomes. Suggest a sensitivity analysis and a plan for primary and exploratory outcomes.

keyConcepts.explanation: The probability of at least one false positive can rise as more hypotheses are tested. When controlling familywise error, Bonferroni is valid without independence and can be conservative. False discovery rate controls a different quantity.

MCAR means missingness does not depend on observed or unobserved data. Under MAR it can depend on observed data but not the missing value after conditioning on them. Under MNAR it can depend on the missing value even after conditioning.

Multiple imputation pools uncertainty across plausible completed data sets under an explicit model. It does not repair poor measurement or prove MAR. Model-based sensitivity can vary assumptions about unobserved outcomes; bounds show what is possible without such assumptions.

A bootstrap can approximate sampling uncertainty if it reflects how data were collected. Resample independent units such as clusters or people, keeping related observations together. Resampling cannot correct systematic bias by itself.
Prespecify primary outcomes and analysis where appropriate. Record denominator, exclusions, missingness, code, versions and sensitivity analyses without exposing identifiers.

misconceptions.claim: A non-significant result proves no effect.
misconceptions.correction: Read the effect estimates, intervals, power and assumptions; absence of evidence is not evidence of no meaningful effect.

misconceptions.claim: Twenty significant-looking confidence intervals fix missing data.
misconceptions.correction: Intervals address a sampling model, and choosing among many analyses adds uncertainty rather than fixing the missing-outcome mechanism.

workedExample.design: Fictional trial: 8 events observed among 90 followed treated participants and 12 among 90 control; each group originally had 100. Separately, imagine 20 independent tests each with a true null.
workedExample.interpretation: The chance of at least one false positive is about 64.2% in the stated family. The possible treated-minus-control risk difference is −14 to +6 percentage points under extreme missing outcomes. These are logical bounds, not confidence limits.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Describe why neither a P value nor a narrower confidence interval can resolve uncertainty about missing outcomes. Suggest a sensitivity analysis and a plan for primary and exploratory outcomes.
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Report the missing counts per group, reason about likely mechanisms, and show extremes and plausible alternatives. Match error control to the scientific decision; label exploratory results.

rProgression.menus: Use grouped counts to confirm the observed denominators before analysing.
rProgression.bridge: Compute the familywise probability and missing-outcome bounds in R.
rProgression.coding: Vary the number of unobserved events in each arm. Observe when the sign of the effect changes.

practiceQuestions.objective: Calculate the familywise error probability under independent true nulls.
practiceQuestions.stem: Twenty independent tests all have true null hypotheses. Each rejects falsely with probability 0.05. What is the probability of at least one false rejection?

options.feedback: This is the probability for a single test.
This is close to the probability of no false rejections.
The probability should be calculated from the complement.
The complement of 0.95 to the 20th power is about 0.642.
The expected number of false rejections is one; that does not mean at least one is certain.

practiceQuestions.hint: Calculate the probability all 20 avoid a false rejection.
practiceQuestions.lesson: A familywise error rate concerns at least one error among a set of tests.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Under independence the probability is 1 − 0.95^20 ≈ 64.2%. Under dependence this formula generally changes.

lessons.title: Choose a study design and comparison group
lessons.objective: Identify what a study can estimate from how it sampled participants and measured outcomes.
lessons.summary: Start with a question and the source population. The design determines the comparison, useful denominator and threats to validity. Interviews and other qualitative methods can explain experiences that a risk estimate alone cannot.
lessons.challenge: Explain whom you would recruit as controls and what information you would need to estimate disease occurrence.
lessons.steps: For a fictional case-control study, calculate the exposure odds ratio using the cross-product. Decide what would happen if twice as many controls were sampled in the same exposure proportions.
lessons.r:
tab <- rbind(cases=c(exposed=40,unexposed=20),controls=c(exposed=20,unexposed=40))
or <- function(x) x[1,1]*x[2,2]/(x[1,2]*x[2,1])
doubled <- tab
doubled[2,] <- 2*doubled[2,]
stopifnot(or(tab)==4,or(doubled)==4,
          isTRUE(all.equal(c(sum(tab[1,])/sum(tab),sum(doubled[1,])/sum(doubled)),c(.5,1/3))))
print(tab)
print(c(odds_ratio=or(tab),odds_ratio_more_controls=or(doubled)))

learningObjectives: Identify what a study can estimate from how it sampled participants and measured outcomes.
Explain whom you would recruit as controls and what information you would need to estimate disease occurrence.

keyConcepts.explanation: Case reports and series can generate hypotheses. Cross-sectional surveys measure status at a point or period. A cohort starts from a defined population or exposure and can estimate risk or rate if denominators and follow-up are known.

Controls represent the exposure experience of the source population that produced the cases, with exact requirements depending on sampling. In ordinary cumulative sampling the association is an odds ratio, which approximates a risk ratio under rare-outcome conditions. With risk-set sampling the appropriate odds-ratio analysis estimates a rate ratio without that assumption.

In a case-crossover study, compare exposure in a defined hazard window before an acute event with exposure during control windows for the same person. Time trends and choice of windows can bias the result.

Interrupted time series examines level or trend changes against a projected baseline. Difference in differences compares pre/post changes against a comparison group; it relies on a credible parallel trend in the absence of intervention, among other assumptions.

Interviews or observations can investigate mechanisms, experience and implementation. Sample for adequate depth and perspective. Mixed methods deliberately integrate qualitative and quantitative findings; qualitative themes are not population percentages.

misconceptions.claim: Any people without the disease can be controls.
misconceptions.correction: Controls should be chosen from people who could have produced a recorded case under the study definition.

misconceptions.claim: Matching eliminates confounding automatically.
misconceptions.correction: Analyse the matching as designed and consider whether matching variables were appropriate. It does not address unmeasured confounding.

workedExample.design: Fictional case-control study of an acute reaction. Forty cases were exposed and 20 unexposed. Twenty sampled controls were exposed and 40 unexposed. The study chose the numbers of cases and controls.
workedExample.interpretation: The exposure odds ratio is (40 × 40)/(20 × 20) = 4. Doubling both control counts still gives 4. The case fraction in the recruited sample changes from 1/2 to 1/3; neither fraction estimates population disease risk.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Explain whom you would recruit as controls and what information you would need to estimate disease occurrence.
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Identify the design from how participants entered. State who was eligible at the same sites and times and whether exposure was ascertained comparably. Name a likely source of bias before interpreting the odds ratio.

rProgression.menus: Compare case and control counts in a 2 × 2 table. For matched cases use a method that respects pairing.
rProgression.bridge: Use the cross-product in R to check the odds ratio, keeping the row and column labels.
rProgression.coding: Change the fraction of controls sampled and explain why risks still cannot be read from these four cells.
