practiceQuestions.objective: Identify controls from the population that produced the cases.
practiceQuestions.stem: A clinic studies whether an exposure is associated with an acute condition using a case-control design. Cases are residents of its catchment who developed the condition during one year. Which criterion matters most for selecting controls?

options.text: They had no exposure of interest.
options.feedback: Selecting on exposure can distort the comparison.

options.text: Their age exactly equals the mean age of the cases.
options.feedback: Source population membership is central. Matching is optional and does not mean selecting the case-group mean.

options.text: They come from people who could have been identified as cases had they developed the condition that year.
options.feedback: Controls should reflect the relevant population and time at risk.

options.text: They are from a different region with no access to the clinic.
options.feedback: The region may have a different exposure distribution and different case ascertainment.

options.text: Their number equals the number of cases.
options.feedback: The number of controls concerns precision, not the fundamental selection criterion.

practiceQuestions.hint: Ask where the cases came from before matching or counting controls.
practiceQuestions.lesson: Controls provide a comparison of exposure in a specified source population.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Controls should come from the source population that generated the cases under the study's eligibility and ascertainment rules.

lessons.title: Interim analyses and reproducible research
lessons.objective: Recognise why repeated looks need a plan, and identify what makes a statistical result reproducible and suitable to share.
lessons.summary: Prespecify the analysis and monitoring where appropriate. Record which data and code produced each result, explain departures and protect participants' privacy. Keep exploratory work clearly labelled. In drug development, use the study phase to identify its intended purpose, then judge what the design and results can support.
lessons.challenge: Explain how you would monitor harm, assess bias, and share the analysis without sending identifiable participant data.
lessons.steps: Compare one test at 0.05 with an illustration of two independent tests at 0.05. Actual interim analyses usually reuse accumulating data and are dependent. Plan monitoring with a statistician and an independent monitoring committee as appropriate.
lessons.r:
p <- .05
twice <- 1-(1-p)^2
bonf <- 1-(1-p/2)^2
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(twice,2*p-p^2)),abs(twice-.0975)<1e-12,
          abs(bonf-.049375)<1e-12)
print(c(one=p,two_independent=twice,two_independent_split=bonf))

learningObjectives: Recognise why repeated looks need a plan, and identify what makes a statistical result reproducible and suitable to share.
Explain how you would monitor harm, assess bias, and share the analysis without sending identifiable participant data.
Distinguish the typical purposes of drug trial phases from the evidence needed for a specific claim.

keyConcepts.explanation: Testing repeatedly and stopping at the first conventional P value can inflate the false-positive probability. Group-sequential designs prespecify looks and boundaries, for example using alpha spending. Their calculations account for planned information and dependence.

An ethics committee or IRB reviews participant protections. A monitoring committee may review accruing confidential evidence and recommend continuing, modifying or stopping a trial under its charter. These roles are distinct.

Register the study as appropriate, state recruitment and consent procedures, prespecify outcomes, exclusions and analyses, and report deviations and adverse events. Share code, definitions and a usable data description under the project's governance rules.

Collect only necessary data. Replacing names with codes does not by itself make data anonymous. Use synthetic data to demonstrate an analysis, and use authorised access for sensitive records. Disclose relevant conflicts and funding.

Phase 1 usually examines tolerability, dose and how the body handles the drug. Phase 2 explores preliminary benefit, dosing and harms in people with the condition. Phase 3 typically evaluates efficacy and adverse effects more definitively. Phase 4 studies after approval can examine safety and effectiveness in wider or longer use.

misconceptions.claim: Stop as soon as the usual P < 0.05 appears at any look.
misconceptions.correction: Use a prespecified monitoring plan. Do not apply the single-look threshold to an arbitrary sequence of looks.

misconceptions.claim: Removing names means all rows are safe to share.
misconceptions.correction: Dates, uncommon combinations, locations and free text can identify participants. Follow project data-sharing approvals.

workedExample.design: Teaching probability model with two independent opportunities to reject a true null at 5%. It illustrates repetition and is not a model of the dependence in an actual staged clinical trial.
workedExample.interpretation: One rejection probability is 5%; at least one across two independent tests is 1 − 0.95² = 9.75%. A Bonferroni split of 0.025 per test caps this two-test familywise probability at 5%; for this independent example it is about 4.94%. This is not a recommendation for trial boundaries.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Explain how you would monitor harm, assess bias, and share the analysis without sending identifiable participant data.
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Distinguish protocol and statistical analysis plan from independent monitoring and the ethics review. Explain what evidence would be examined, when and by whom. Share synthetic data, code and assumptions for practice.

teachingPrompts.prompt: A press release calls a small uncontrolled phase 2 study proof that a medicine prevents admission. What can you conclude?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Phase 2 can inform further evaluation. Look at the design, comparator, endpoint, follow-up, estimates and uncertainty before drawing conclusions about hospital admission.

rProgression.menus: Use the fictional calculation to discuss what is prespecified rather than to monitor a real trial.
rProgression.bridge: Compute the complementary probability in base R and verify it against the two-test union rule.
rProgression.coding: Change the per-test threshold, then explain why shared participants break the independent-tests calculation.

practiceQuestions.objective: Explain why single-test thresholds cannot be reused at every interim look.
practiceQuestions.stem: A study plans to inspect accumulating outcome data each month and stop for efficacy at the first unadjusted P < 0.05. What is the main statistical concern with this rule?

options.text: The repeated looks can inflate the chance of a false positive.
options.feedback: A planned sequential design can control this probability while allowing monitoring.

options.text: Each look must be independent because a new month has passed.
options.feedback: The data commonly overlap across looks.

options.text: The null hypothesis automatically changes with each look.
options.feedback: The same hypothesis may be tested repeatedly.

options.text: A smaller P value always identifies the right treatment decision.
options.feedback: Results must account for monitoring and be interpreted alongside effects and harms.

options.text: An ethics review alone adjusts the significance level.
options.feedback: Ethical and statistical oversight are related but distinct.

practiceQuestions.hint: How many opportunities are there to stop by chance?
practiceQuestions.lesson: Specify how repeated looks and stopping rules affect inference before trial results are known.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Repeated stopping opportunities can inflate the false-positive probability. Use a prespecified group-sequential or other suitable monitoring method that accounts for dependence.

lessons.title: Comparing three or more independent groups
lessons.objective: Choose and interpret an overall group test and comparisons that answer the study question.
lessons.summary: Start with one independent outcome per person and decide whether the question concerns means or a broader difference in distributions. Ordinary one-way ANOVA compares means using within-group variation to judge how far the group means differ. Its classical F test assumes independent errors, approximate within-group normality and a common variance. Inspect group plots and residuals in context. Welch one-way ANOVA compares means without imposing a common variance. Kruskal–Wallis pools and ranks observations from independent groups. Its null concerns group distributions, and a location-shift interpretation needs comparable shapes. A small omnibus P value supports a difference somewhere. Report the direction, size and uncertainty for relevant contrasts. Define planned contrasts and the comparison family in advance, and account for multiplicity when drawing several inferences.
lessons.challenge: The overall test is significant. A colleague wants to claim the written group improved more than usual training. Which comparison and uncertainty would you report for that claim?
lessons.steps: Eight different staff in each of three fictional training groups complete a common scored simulation. Select the three columns and choose Analysis → Analysis of Variance → One Way. Mean improvement scores are 5.5, 7.0 and 9.0 points for usual, written and coached training. The ordinary overall F statistic is 10.79 with 2 and 21 degrees of freedom. The coached-minus-usual difference is 3.5 points, with an approximate Tukey 95% simultaneous interval of 1.59 to 5.41 points for all pairwise comparisons. In the One Way report use the equality-of-variance/Welch follow-on or run Welch in R. In a separate analysis of the same data, Kruskal–Wallis yields H = 11.59 after adjusting for ties. Compare what the tests ask and what the effect estimates mean.
lessons.r:
# Fictional scores from different people, one outcome per participant.
scores <- data.frame(Usual = c(4, 7, 5, 6, 8, 3, 5, 6),
                     Written = c(6, 8, 9, 7, 5, 7, 8, 6),
                     Coached = c(7, 9, 11, 8, 9, 10, 7, 11))
long <- stack(scores)
names(long) <- c("improvement", "training")
ordinary <- aov(improvement ~ training, data = long)
ordinary_table <- summary(ordinary)[[1]]
welch <- oneway.test(improvement ~ training, data = long, var.equal = FALSE)
ranks <- kruskal.test(improvement ~ training, data = long)
contrasts <- TukeyHSD(ordinary, conf.level = 0.95)$training
print(colMeans(scores))
print(ordinary_table)
print(welch)
print(ranks)
print(contrasts)
stopifnot(all(colMeans(scores) == c(5.5, 7, 9)),
          abs(ordinary_table[["F value"]][1] - 259/24) < 1e-10,
          abs(unname(welch$statistic) - 9.169989182507) < 1e-9,
          abs(unname(ranks$statistic) - 11.58812749889) < 1e-9,
          abs(contrasts["Coached-Usual", "diff"] - 3.5) < 1e-12,
          max(abs(contrasts["Coached-Usual", c("lwr","upr")] - c(1.594628, 5.405372))) < 1e-6)
boxplot(improvement ~ training, data = long, ylab = "Improvement (points)",
        main = "Fictional training groups")
plot(fitted(ordinary), residuals(ordinary), xlab = "Fitted improvement",
     ylab = "Residual", main = "Check within-group spread")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey50")

learningObjectives: Distinguish an overall equality-of-means test from a rank comparison.
Choose ordinary or Welch ANOVA using independence and group spread.
Interpret an omnibus result with prespecified contrasts or adjusted pairwise estimates.
Recognise when investigators are adjusting for a covariate or jointly comparing distinct outcomes.

keyConcepts.explanation: A global test addresses all group means or distributions together under the chosen model.
Tukey intervals have simultaneous coverage for the family of all pairwise differences in the ordinary ANOVA setting. Other comparison plans can call for a different method.
For a continuous outcome, this compares groups after adjustment for covariates such as baseline score. A common-slope model assumes the group contrast is constant across the covariate range.
This compares vectors of means for several outcomes jointly. A global result needs outcome-specific interpretation and follow-up appropriate to the study plan.

misconceptions.claim: A significant ANOVA proves every pair differs.
misconceptions.correction: The overall test supports at least one difference under the model. Each specific claim needs its own contrast and appropriate uncertainty.

misconceptions.claim: Kruskal–Wallis is an assumption-free test of medians.
misconceptions.correction: Independence and appropriate sampling still matter. Rank differences can reflect shape or spread as well as location.

misconceptions.claim: Any three groups should be analysed with three unadjusted t tests.
misconceptions.correction: Use a comparison family aligned to the question. Several unadjusted tests inflate the chance of a false positive across the family.

workedExample.design: Fictional parallel comparison of three training formats. Different people contribute a single improvement score each. The worksheet columns are independent groups and rows need no matching.
workedExample.interpretation: The ordinary and Welch analyses support a difference among means. The rank test gives evidence of a group difference on the rank scale. The Tukey interval estimates coached minus usual as 3.5 points with simultaneous 95% limits of about 1.59 and 5.41. The written-minus-usual Tukey interval includes zero.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why can an overall ANOVA P value be small when one pairwise interval crosses zero?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: The global null requires all means to be equal. Evidence against it can be driven by some comparisons while others remain uncertain.

teachingPrompts.prompt: If the coached group contains much more variable responses, what changes about your choice of method and reporting?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Inspect whether variability or outliers reflect plausible observations. Welch can target mean differences despite unequal variances. Report spreads and appropriate contrasts and intervals.

teachingPrompts.prompt: The three group distributions have similar medians but differ in shape and skew. If Kruskal–Wallis is significant, what conclusion is supported?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: There is evidence of a difference on the rank scale. Differences in shape make a pure location or median interpretation unwarranted.

rProgression.menus: Use Analysis → Analysis of Variance → One Way with the three group columns. Tukey and the Welch/equality-of-variance follow-on are separate analyses. Use Kruskal–Wallis for the independent rank comparison.
rProgression.bridge: Compare the ordinary F statistic and degrees of freedom with aov. Compare the tie-adjusted Kruskal–Wallis result with kruskal.test. Compare Tukey differences using the same group order, confidence level and simultaneous method.
rProgression.coding: Increase one coached score and inspect how the mean, spread and each overall result change. Explain which population contrast still answers the scientific question.

lessons.title: Comparing three or more repeated conditions
lessons.topic: Participant blocks, repeated-measures ANOVA and Friedman
lessons.objective: Use matching to compare conditions and recognise when a longitudinal model is needed.
lessons.summary: When every person contributes one result under each of several conditions, the person is a block. Dependence within a person is part of the design. A one-factor repeated-measures ANOVA addresses mean differences and assigns variability to participant and within-participant strata. The ordinary uncorrected F reference assumes independent participants, appropriate normal within-participant contrasts and sphericity for three or more conditions. Sphericity means equal variances of pairwise within-person differences. Friedman ranks conditions within independent complete blocks and asks whether the conditions systematically differ in rank. It does not estimate a mean difference. For related binary outcomes, Cochran Q compares response probabilities across matched conditions. Incomplete trajectories, irregular times or a treatment-by-time question need the appropriate longitudinal model and assumptions about missingness. Dropping incomplete rows can change who the analysis represents.
lessons.challenge: A follow-up study measures each person at baseline, 2 months and 6 months. Some people miss visits and the study asks whether the trajectory differs by care pathway. Why does a complete-block test answer a narrower question?
lessons.steps: In this fictional comparison, eight clinicians each complete comparable documentation tasks using three interfaces in counterbalanced order. Each worksheet row is one clinician and each column one interface. Select the three columns and choose Analysis → Analysis of Variance → Two Way for this complete additive participant-block example. Mean times are 51.50, 48.50 and 46.25 seconds. The condition F statistic is 22.2 with 2 and 14 degrees of freedom. Run Friedman on the same matched columns. Base R reports rank statistic 10.75 and a chi-square P value near 0.00463. The StatsDirect Friedman report uses an Iman–Davenport F approximation for its P value. The R code prints both approximations. With only eight clinicians, an assignment-respecting exact or simulated rank test can be useful if exchangeability within blocks is justified. If C versus A was the single prespecified contrast, the mean within-clinician difference is −5.25 seconds with an ordinary paired 95% interval of about −7.19 to −3.31. An analysis of several paired contrasts needs an appropriate multiplicity plan.
lessons.r:
# Fictional documentation times, one row per clinician and one column per interface.
times <- cbind(A = c(52, 47, 54, 43, 62, 51, 55, 48),
               B = c(48, 45, 52, 38, 58, 47, 51, 49),
               C = c(45, 46, 49, 37, 55, 48, 47, 43))
participants <- nrow(times)
conditions <- ncol(times)
long <- data.frame(seconds = as.vector(times),
                   interface = factor(rep(colnames(times), each = participants)),
                   clinician = factor(rep(seq_len(participants), times = conditions)))
fit <- aov(seconds ~ interface + Error(clinician/interface), data = long)
within <- summary(fit)[["Error: clinician:interface"]][[1]]
ranks <- friedman.test(times)
rank_statistic <- unname(ranks$statistic)
# The StatsDirect Help specifies the Iman–Davenport F reference for Friedman.
df1 <- conditions - 1
df2 <- (participants - 1)*df1
rank_f <- (participants - 1)*rank_statistic/(participants*df1 - rank_statistic)
rank_f_p <- pf(rank_f, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)
planned <- t.test(times[, "C"] - times[, "A"])
print(colMeans(times))
print(summary(fit))
print(ranks)
print(c(Iman_Davenport_F = rank_f, Iman_Davenport_P = rank_f_p))
print(planned)
stopifnot(all(colMeans(times) == c(51.5, 48.5, 46.25)),
          all(within[["Df"]] == c(2, 14)),
          abs(within[["F value"]][1] - 22.2) < 1e-10,
          abs(rank_statistic - 10.75) < 1e-12,
          abs(ranks$p.value - pchisq(10.75, 2, lower.tail = FALSE)) < 1e-12,
          abs(rank_f - 43/3) < 1e-12,
          abs(rank_f_p - 0.0004095201) < 1e-9,
          abs(unname(planned$estimate) + 5.25) < 1e-12,
          max(abs(planned$conf.int - c(-7.185012, -3.314988))) < 1e-6)
matplot(seq_len(conditions), t(times), type = "b", lty = 1, pch = 16,
        col = "grey55", xaxt = "n", xlab = "Interface", ylab = "Time (seconds)")
axis(1, at = seq_len(conditions), labels = colnames(times))

learningObjectives: Recognise participant as the block and preserve row alignment across repeated conditions.
Distinguish a mean comparison by repeated-measures ANOVA from the within-block rank test.
Explain sphericity and choose a different model when design, follow-up or missingness requires it.
Select an analysis for matched binary outcomes.

keyConcepts.explanation: A person contributes several observations but still represents one participant. Compare like conditions within each row.

For an uncorrected univariate repeated-measures F test, the variance of the within-person difference is assumed to be the same for each pair of conditions. Corrections such as Greenhouse–Geisser adjust reference degrees of freedom under departures.
Friedman ranks within each participant and requires a usable observation per condition for each included block. Inference still depends on sampling and design.
Define the desired group difference or trajectory first. A suitable repeated-data model can incorporate correlation, visit times and covariates, under justified assumptions.

misconceptions.claim: An equal number of observations in each condition makes them independent groups.
misconceptions.correction: The data are related because the same people supplied each observation. A worksheet layout cannot change that design.

misconceptions.claim: Friedman handles arbitrary missing visits or different visit schedules.
misconceptions.correction: The usual Friedman analysis compares complete matched blocks. Other missing-data designs require methods aligned to the outcome and study question.

misconceptions.claim: Repeated-measures ANOVA and Friedman must give the same P value.
misconceptions.correction: They use different targets and statistics. Even for Friedman, different reference approximations can give different P values for the same set of ranks.

workedExample.design: Fictional eight-person, three-condition complete within-person example. Each person contributes one comparable task per interface and participants are independent. For interpretation assume the task and counterbalancing have controlled relevant order effects.
workedExample.interpretation: The mean time is lowest for C. The paired C-minus-A contrast estimates 5.25 seconds shorter on average. The rank and mean analyses both indicate differences among interfaces under their respective assumptions. The sample and design do not establish general performance on other tasks.

teachingPrompts.prompt: What would go wrong if you sorted the three columns independently before testing?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Rows would stop representing the same clinician, so paired differences and within-row ranks would no longer reflect the study design.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Would a significant condition effect show that the learning curve differs across interfaces?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: The test compares conditions in the stated blocked design. A learning-curve question requires an appropriate design and a model for interface, order or time and their interaction.

rProgression.menus: Run Analysis → Analysis of Variance → Two Way on the three condition columns. Then run Friedman on the same complete, aligned rows. The worksheet has no replicate observations within clinician–interface cells.
rProgression.bridge: Compare the condition F statistic against the within-participant ANOVA table. For Friedman, compare the within-row rank statistic and use the Iman–Davenport line to match the application's P convention.
rProgression.coding: Plot each clinician's three times in R. Calculate the standard deviations of the three within-person differences. Treat these eight observations as an illustration of sphericity, not a definitive diagnostic.

lessons.title: Estimating uncertainty in a complex survey
lessons.topic: Design weights and primary sampling units
lessons.objective: Estimate a population proportion and its design-based standard error in a stratified cluster sample.
lessons.summary: The sampling design determines the point estimate and its uncertainty. A design weight expands an observed unit by the inverse of its selection probability. In this example clinics are randomly sampled separately within two strata and everyone in a selected clinic is observed. Each clinic contains the same number of eligible people. The estimated stratum proportion is the average of its sampled clinic proportions. For each stratum, estimate the variance of that average from variation between sampled clinics, divided by the number sampled and multiplied by the finite population correction. Then add the independent stratum variances weighted by the square of each stratum's population share.
lessons.steps: A fictional survey frame contains 12 urban and 4 rural clinics, each serving 100 eligible people. Independently in each stratum, sample clinics by simple random sampling without replacement: 4 urban clinics with 10, 20, 30 and 40 people with the outcome, and 2 rural clinics with 40 and 80. The urban estimate is 25% and the rural estimate is 60%. The known population shares of 75% and 25% give an overall estimate of 33.75%, compared with the unweighted 36.67%. The design-based standard error is 5.30 percentage points. Only two rural clinics were sampled, so variance estimates and approximate intervals can be fragile.
lessons.challenge: Imagine a design that randomly samples people within each selected clinic as well. What extra information would you need to estimate uncertainty?
learningObjectives: Identify the strata, primary sampling units and inclusion probabilities.
Compute a design-weighted proportion and use the finite population correction.
Explain why correct survey uncertainty needs the sample design as well as weights.

keyConcepts.explanation: Here each urban respondent represents 12/4 = 3 people and each rural respondent represents 4/2 = 2 people. All enrolled people in selected clinics were observed.

The sampled clinics supply independent stratum estimates because each stratum was sampled separately. Within a stratum, use the sample variance of clinic proportions times (1 − n/N)/n, where N is the number of clinics on the frame and n the number sampled.
A subgroup such as younger people is a domain, rarely a separate probability sample. In general, retain the survey design and indicate domain membership when estimating uncertainty.

misconceptions.claim: The survey contains 600 independently selected people.
misconceptions.correction: The first-stage selections were six clinics. The independent-person standard error does not capture the design.

misconceptions.claim: A table of final person weights is sufficient for the standard error.
misconceptions.correction: Use design strata and primary sampling units, with finite population information for this example. Some surveys instead provide replicate weights and instructions.

workedExample.design: Stratified single-stage cluster sample of equal-size clinics, with complete enumeration in selected clinics.
workedExample.interpretation: Weighting estimates the proportion among the 1,600 people in the frame. The finite population correction accounts for sizable fractions of clinics sampled. The formula applies to this specific design and does not cover unequal clinic sizes, a second sampling stage, or missing responses.

teachingPrompts.prompt: What changes if all rural clinics are observed?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: There is no sampling variance from rural clinic selection because its sampling fraction equals one. The urban contribution remains.

rProgression.menus: Read the Population Survey help for simple sample-size planning. Use Explore in R for this design-based example.
rProgression.bridge: Match each variance contribution in the output to its population share, clinic variability and sampling fraction.
rProgression.coding: Set all observed rural clinic proportions equal and check how the estimated between-clinic variance contribution changes.

lessons.r:
stratum <- rep(c("Urban","Rural"), c(4,2))
cases <- c(10,20,30,40,40,80)
clinic_size <- 100
N <- c(Urban = 12, Rural = 4)
p_clinic <- split(cases/clinic_size, factor(stratum, levels = names(N)))
n <- lengths(p_clinic)
W <- N/sum(N)
weight <- N[stratum]/n[stratum]
p_h <- vapply(p_clinic, mean, numeric(1))
s2 <- vapply(p_clinic, var, numeric(1))
pieces <- W^2 * (1 - n/N) * s2/n
p <- sum(W*p_h)
se <- sqrt(sum(pieces))
stopifnot(abs(p - 0.3375) < 1e-10,
          abs(p - weighted.mean(cases/clinic_size, weight)) < 1e-10,
          abs(sum(pieces) - 0.0028125) < 1e-10,
          abs(mean(cases/clinic_size) - 220/600) < 1e-10)
print(data.frame(population_share = W, estimate = p_h,
                 sampling_fraction = n/N, variance_contribution = pieces))
print(c(weighted_proportion = p, unweighted_proportion = mean(cases/clinic_size),
        design_standard_error_pp = 100*se))

lessons.title: Interpreting an interrupted time series
lessons.topic: Trends, intervention timing and count denominators
lessons.objective: Interpret immediate changes and trend changes in a rate after a defined intervention.
lessons.summary: An interrupted time series compares observations after an intervention with the projected pre-intervention trend. Choose the expected timing and shape of the change before looking at the outcome. The fitted model can give a level change at the first post-intervention month and a change in slope after that date. Seasonal variation and serial correlation are common. Compare like seasons, examine residuals and use a suitable model for inference. For count outcomes, use a rate with the population at risk or other appropriate exposure. A count regression can include log exposure as an offset.
lessons.steps: A fictional care network changes a reporting process at the start of month 13. It has 24 months of recorded incidents and visit totals. In Explore in R, display incidents per 1,000 visits. A descriptive segmented regression accounts for calendar quarter and gives more weight to months with more visits. The fitted pre-intervention trend rises by 0.69 incidents per 1,000 visits per month. At month 13 the fitted level falls by 2.45 per 1,000 visits relative to continuing the pre-intervention pattern. The slope changes by −1.98 per 1,000 visits per month, giving a post-intervention slope of −1.29. Four months after the change, the fitted contrast is −10.38 per 1,000 visits against the projected baseline. The programme may have changed what is recorded as well as the event frequency.
lessons.challenge: What if a new recording rule and a change in patient case mix took effect on the same date? What additional data could help interpret the apparent change?
learningObjectives: Distinguish a pre-intervention slope, immediate level change and change in slope.
Check whether changing denominators, measurement or seasons could explain a rate change.
Describe the role of serial correlation and a comparison series.

keyConcepts.explanation: Project the fitted pre-intervention trend into the post-intervention period, including the seasonal terms. The contrast is meaningful only if that projection is credible under no intervention.
Nearby residuals can be related. If so, standard errors from an independent-error regression need not be reliable.
If more people are observed or the exposure time rises, an unchanged event rate can produce more events.

misconceptions.claim: The post-intervention slope is the slope-change coefficient.
misconceptions.correction: Add the slope-change coefficient to the original slope.

misconceptions.claim: A fitted break establishes that the intervention caused it.
misconceptions.correction: Coincident events and measurement changes may create similar patterns. A suitable comparison series and design checks can strengthen interpretation.

workedExample.design: Fictional monthly rates and visits, one intervention date, seasonal quarter indicators, descriptive weighted least squares.
workedExample.interpretation: The fitted contrast combines a level change and a slope change. Weights give more influence to larger visit totals. No confidence interval or causal claim is made from this model. In practice consider more time points, a pre-specified seasonal model, serial dependence and a defensible comparison series.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why is the effect four months later different from the first post-intervention month's contrast?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: At the first post month, time since intervention is zero. Four months later the contrast also includes four months of the change in trend.

rProgression.menus: Read Multiple Linear Regression help for interpreting coefficients. Run this segmented rate example with Explore in R.
rProgression.bridge: Compare the fitted line and the projected pre-intervention line on the plot.
rProgression.coding: Set post and after to zero only in the prediction data. Explain why this retains the seasonal counterfactual.

lessons.r:
month <- 1:24
time <- month - 13
post <- as.integer(time >= 0)
after <- pmax(time, 0)
quarter <- factor(((month - 1) %% 12) %/% 3 + 1)
visits <- 1000 * (1 + month %% 5)
events <- c(44,66,88,110,24,46,66,96,115,28,56,84,
            104,135,25,46,60,80,75,16,28,45,60,60)
d <- data.frame(month, time, post, after, quarter, visits, events)
d$rate <- 1000 * d$events / d$visits
fit <- lm(rate ~ time + post + after + quarter, weights = visits, data = d)
b <- coef(fit)
no_change <- transform(d, post = 0L, after = 0)
projected <- predict(fit, newdata = no_change)
print(round(c(pre_slope = b[["time"]], level_change = b[["post"]],
              slope_change = b[["after"]],
              post_slope = b[["time"]] + b[["after"]],
              contrast_month17 = b[["post"]] + 4*b[["after"]]), 2))
stopifnot(abs(b[["post"]] + 2.4476868) < 1e-6,
          abs(b[["time"]] + b[["after"]] + 1.2882036) < 1e-6,
          abs(fitted(fit)[17] - projected[17] + 10.378659) < 1e-5)
plot(d$month, d$rate, xlab = "Month", ylab = "Recorded incidents per 1,000 visits",
     main = "Fictional intervention and monthly recorded incidents", pch = 16)
lines(d$month, fitted(fit), col = "navy", lwd = 2)
lines(d$month, projected, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
abline(v = 13, lty = 3)
legend("topleft", c("Fitted trend", "Projected without intervention"),
       col = c("navy","firebrick"), lty = c(1,2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

options.text: −4.0 per 1,000 visits

lessons.title: Reading small-area disease maps
lessons.topic: Maps, standardisation and uncertain local rates
lessons.objective: Choose a suitable denominator and interpret differences in area rates without overinterpreting rankings.
lessons.summary: A map of counts can show where services might face more demand. Comparing frequency across areas usually calls for rates based on comparable populations, periods and case definitions. If age distributions differ, compare age-specific rates or use the same standard population in every area. Small areas can have highly variable rates. Display uncertainty where possible and follow data disclosure rules. An area-level association does not establish an association for the individuals in those areas.
lessons.steps: In a fictional year, Area A records 46 first diagnoses among 10,000 residents at risk and Area B records 52 among 8,000. Their crude rates are 4.6 and 6.5 per 1,000. With complete follow-up and at most one first diagnosis per person, these are one-year risks per 1,000 residents. Standardise their age-specific rates to an equal split of younger and older residents. The age-standardised rates are 7.0 and 5.0 per 1,000, reversing their crude ranking. Area C records only two diagnoses among 150 residents. Its crude rate is 13.3 per 1,000, with a wide 95% Poisson interval of about 1.6 to 48.2. This interval assumes a fixed denominator and a Poisson count model. The R example displays counts and crude rates on schematic maps and gives the standardised rates in a table.
lessons.challenge: A district has a high recorded disease rate and more clinics per resident. How would you investigate differential detection before interpreting this pattern?
learningObjectives: Match the numerator, denominator, place and observation period.
Separate crude rates, standardised comparisons and statistical uncertainty.
Identify problems from small counts, map boundaries and ecological interpretation.

keyConcepts.explanation: Counts may help with service planning. For contrasting places, rates account for differences in population size and can be standardised for age or another chosen factor.
With few diagnoses, one additional case can move the estimate considerably. Colour alone gives no sense of that uncertainty.
Area definitions can change the pattern. Very small cells may risk identification, so apply the data provider's disclosure rules. Suppressed or missing values must remain distinguishable from zero.

misconceptions.claim: The darkest area necessarily has the highest true rate.
misconceptions.correction: The colour displays an estimated rate under chosen categories. Check the denominator, uncertainty and comparability before ranking areas.

misconceptions.claim: A district-level association tells us which individuals are at risk.
misconceptions.correction: Area summaries can hide variation and do not identify individual exposures or effects.

workedExample.design: Four fictional areas with complete one-year follow-up and age-specific diagnosis counts. A 50:50 age mix is applied to every area.
workedExample.interpretation: The crude rates summarise the observed populations. The age-standardised rates compare areas under a common age mix. The simple interval for Area C illustrates small-count uncertainty and does not account for ascertainment, spillover or spatial dependence.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Area C has the highest crude rate and the fewest recorded diagnoses. Which map would help plan clinic workload and which would start a comparison of disease frequency?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Counts describe recorded burden. Rates with uncertainty compare frequency. Adjust age where appropriate and check whether detection differs.

rProgression.menus: Use Direct Standardisation help to review population weighting. Use Explore in R for the schematic maps.
rProgression.bridge: Compare the two panels, then inspect the crude and age-standardised rates in the table.
rProgression.coding: Change the common age weights once and use the same weights for all areas. Recheck the comparison.

lessons.r:
areas <- LETTERS[1:4]
pop <- rbind(A = c(9000,1000), B = c(2000,6000),
             C = c(100,50), D = c(4000,1000))
count <- rbind(A = c(36,10), B = c(4,48), C = c(1,1), D = c(8,4))
total <- rowSums(count)
crude <- 1000 * total / rowSums(pop)
standard <- drop(1000 * (count/pop) %*% c(.5,.5))
C_interval <- 1000 * poisson.test(total["C"], T = sum(pop["C",]))$conf.int
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(crude[1:2]), c(4.6,6.5))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(standard[1:2]), c(7,5))),
          abs(crude["C"] - 1000*2/150) < 1e-10,
          all(abs(C_interval - c(1.614729,48.164584)) < 1e-5))
print(data.frame(area = areas, diagnoses = total, residents = rowSums(pop),
                 crude_per_1000 = round(crude,1), standard_per_1000 = round(standard,1)))
print(round(setNames(C_interval, c("C lower 95%", "C upper 95%")),1))
# Equal rectangles are a schematic, without real boundaries or identifiers.
map <- function(value, heading, breaks, dp) {
  plot.new()
  plot.window(xlim = c(0,2), ylim = c(0,2), asp = 1)
  cols <- c("#eef6fc", "#a7cae3", "#4b8ab9")
  group <- cut(value, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
  x <- c(0,1,0,1)
  y <- c(1,1,0,0)
  rect(x, y, x+1, y+1, col = cols[group], border = "white")
  text(x+.5, y+.5, paste0(areas, "\n", formatC(value, digits = dp, format = "f")))
  title(main = heading, cex.main = 0.9)
}
old <- par(mfrow = c(1,2), mar = c(1,1,3,1))
map(total, "Recorded diagnoses", c(0,15,40,Inf), 0)
map(crude, "Crude per 1,000", c(0,4,8,Inf), 1)
par(old)

lessons.title: Comparing costs and health outcomes
lessons.objective: Compare two programmes using incremental costs and QALYs, and explain how assumptions affect the result.
lessons.summary: A cost-effectiveness model compares a programme with a relevant alternative, commonly current care. State whose costs the analysis counts and how long it follows costs and outcomes. An opportunity cost is the benefit forgone when resources cannot be used elsewhere. Discounting expresses future costs and health outcomes in present values using the rates specified for the exercise. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio divides additional cost by additional health gain. Use sensitivity analysis to test important assumptions. Compare affordability, equity and implementation separately.
lessons.steps: A fictional care provider compares a new programme with current care over two years. Per participant, programme costs at years 0, 1 and 2 are £800, £160 and £100. Current care costs £400, £100 and £100. The programme yields 0.79 QALYs at the end of each of years 1 and 2, and current care 0.75 each year. Use an illustrative 3% annual discount rate for both costs and QALYs. The increments are about £458 and 0.0765 QALYs, so the ratio is about £5,987 per additional QALY. If the annual gain is 0.02 QALYs instead of 0.04 and costs stay fixed, the ratio rises to about £11,974. This crosses the exercise's fictional £10,000 per QALY benchmark.
lessons.challenge: If unpaid family care falls under the new programme, how might the comparison change if the analysis takes a broader societal perspective?
learningObjectives: Name the comparator, cost perspective and time horizon.
Discount the costs and QALYs and compute the incremental ratio when both increments are positive.
Use a sensitivity analysis and distinguish cost-effectiveness from a budget decision.

keyConcepts.explanation: A care provider's perspective includes costs borne by that provider. A broader analysis may include other costs, such as patient time or unpaid care. A short horizon can miss downstream costs and benefits.
Spending on this programme uses resources that could produce benefits elsewhere. A low ratio alone does not say how much budget is needed or displaced.
If an option costs more and produces worse outcomes than its alternative, it is dominated in this two-option comparison. Do not interpret a negative ratio by ranking it numerically.

misconceptions.claim: The new programme's total cost divided by its total QALYs is its incremental ratio.
misconceptions.correction: Use the difference in costs divided by the difference in QALYs relative to the comparator.

misconceptions.claim: Discounting and sensitivity analysis are equivalent.
misconceptions.correction: Discounting accounts for timing. Sensitivity analysis changes a model assumption to see how much the result depends on it.

workedExample.design: A fictional two-year provider-perspective comparison. Costs and health outcomes are valued at the stated times. The discount rate and benchmark are invented for learning.
workedExample.interpretation: The base case lies below the fictional benchmark. Halving the assumed health gain puts the estimate above it. Possible costs and health gains beyond year two, differential effects across groups and real budget impact are outside the model.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why might options with similar ratios have very different budget impacts?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Budget impact also depends on eligible population, uptake and annual spending. An incremental ratio describes the cost per unit of gain.

rProgression.menus: Review the Population impact lesson to recall how QALYs combine survival and health-related quality. Use Explore in R to calculate the incremental comparison.
rProgression.bridge: Compare the discounted cost and QALY increment to the ratio and the fictional benchmark.
rProgression.coding: Vary the assumed annual QALY gain and find where the ratio crosses the benchmark.

lessons.r:
year <- 0:2
discount <- 1 / (1.03^year)
usual_cost <- c(400,100,100)
programme_cost <- c(800,160,100)
usual_qaly <- c(0,.75,.75)
programme_qaly <- c(0,.79,.79)
dc <- sum((programme_cost-usual_cost)*discount)
dq <- sum((programme_qaly-usual_qaly)*discount)
dq_lower <- sum(c(0,.02,.02)*discount)
benchmark <- 10000
icer <- dc/dq
icer_lower_qaly <- dc/dq_lower
stopifnot(abs(dc - 458.2524272) < 1e-6,
          abs(dq - 0.07653879) < 1e-8,
          abs(icer - 5987.192118) < 0.01,
          icer < benchmark, icer_lower_qaly > benchmark)
print(round(c(cost_increment = dc, QALY_increment = dq,
              cost_per_QALY = icer,
              cost_per_QALY_smaller_gain = icer_lower_qaly), 4))
