questions.objective: Spot a design feature that can bias accuracy estimates.
questions.stem: A clinic compares a new clot marker with imaging. Nearly everyone with a positive marker receives imaging, but most people with a negative marker do not. Investigators report accuracy only for those imaged. Which limitation follows most directly?

options.text: The results have no clinically relevant threshold.
options.feedback: The marker can have a threshold regardless of who receives imaging.

options.text: The verified subset automatically has the intended clinic prevalence.
options.feedback: Selection for imaging depends on the marker result, so its case fraction is not automatically representative.

options.text: A larger sample would remove bias from selective verification.
options.feedback: Larger samples cannot remove systematic selection into verification.

options.text: The design proves the imaging itself causes positive marker results.
options.feedback: Imaging determines the reference classification, but the problem described is selective verification.

options.text: Disease status is incompletely established among marker-negative people, which can bias reported accuracy.
options.feedback: This is partial verification. Disease status is missing for many marker-negative participants because reference verification depends on the index result.

questions.hint: Who does the accuracy table omit, and is that related to their marker result?
questions.lesson: Check how the intended diagnostic population was enrolled and which patients received the reference standard.
questions.explanation: The subset with reference results is selected partly by the index result. Unverified negative patients can include missed cases. The available table cannot simply be treated as if it covered all tested people.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Recognise what discrimination does not tell us about an operating threshold.
questions.stem: A fictional marker's empirical ROC AUC is 0.84, estimated by comparing scores from known cases with known noncases and counting ties as halves. Which interpretation is supported by this value alone?

options.text: At the selected threshold, 84% of positive results are true positives.
options.feedback: That is positive predictive value at a specified cut-off, which also depends on the case mix.

options.text: Any threshold on the curve has 84% sensitivity.
options.feedback: Sensitivity varies with threshold.

options.text: The marker's predicted probabilities match observed disease frequencies.
options.feedback: That is calibration. Ranking performance alone does not establish it.

options.text: It scores a randomly selected case higher than a randomly selected noncase about 84% of the time when ties count as half credit.
options.feedback: Correct. This describes ranking in the evaluated data.

options.text: The optimal treatment decision for each patient follows from 0.84 alone.
options.feedback: Clinical utility depends on threshold, setting and consequences of decisions.

questions.hint: AUC gives a summary of pairwise ranking across thresholds.
questions.lesson: AUC describes discrimination in the evaluated population. It does not establish calibration, predictive value or the best decision rule.
questions.explanation: The empirical AUC equals the fraction of case–noncase pairs correctly ordered plus half the tied fraction. Performance in another population needs separate evidence.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Recognise lead time in an individual example with unchanged death age.
questions.stem: For a fictional condition, screening shifts a person's date of diagnosis from age 67 to 64. Treatment and age at death remain identical. Which phenomenon can explain the apparent three-year increase in survival measured from diagnosis?

options.text: Lead-time bias
options.feedback: Correct. The diagnosis moves earlier but the death does not.

options.text: Length bias
options.feedback: Length bias concerns preferential detection of more slowly progressing conditions. This example follows one unchanged course.

options.text: Verification bias
options.feedback: The example does not concern selective application of a reference standard.

options.text: Loss to follow-up
options.feedback: Death is observed at the same age under both scenarios.

options.text: A treatment effect on mortality
options.feedback: The example explicitly fixes the time of death.

questions.hint: Which event changed, diagnosis or death?
questions.lesson: Looking from diagnosis starts the clock at different times. A programme comparison needs a common start point.
questions.explanation: The added three years reflect earlier recognition. No extension of life follows from comparing survival from diagnosis alone.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Distinguish overdiagnosis from an incorrect result or a false alarm.
questions.stem: A fictional screening test triggers a biopsy. The biopsy correctly identifies a slow-growing lesion. In the hypothetical absence of screening, the lesion would never have caused symptoms or shortened the person's life. Which term best describes detecting it?

options.text: False-positive screening result
options.feedback: There is a real lesion, confirmed by diagnostic assessment.

options.text: Lead-time bias alone
options.feedback: An earlier diagnosis can affect observed survival, but the defining feature here is that the lesion would never matter clinically.

options.text: Overdiagnosis
options.feedback: Correct. The disease is genuinely detected, but would never have caused harm in the person's lifetime.

options.text: False-negative screening result
options.feedback: The lesion was detected.

options.text: Prevented clinical disease
options.feedback: No symptoms would have occurred even without detection.

questions.hint: Does the finding exist, and would it have affected the person's life without screening?
questions.lesson: Overdiagnosis concerns the consequences of detecting real disease. It is distinct from a false positive.
questions.explanation: The hypothetical natural history meets the definition of overdiagnosis. In practice, whether an individual case is overdiagnosed is usually uncertain.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Identify the numerator, denominator and scaling of a maternity indicator.
questions.stem: A fictional annual register uses one consistent definition. It records 9,960 live births, 40 stillbirths, 10 deaths before seven completed days of life and 2 maternal deaths meeting the maternal mortality definition. What is the perinatal mortality rate per 1,000 total births, to two decimal places?

options.feedback: This uses maternal deaths, which do not belong in the perinatal numerator.
This uses stillbirths only, omitting early neonatal deaths.
That is approximately 50/9,960 × 1,000. Perinatal mortality uses total births.
Correct. The 50 perinatal deaths are divided by 10,000 total births, then multiplied by 1,000.
This is the death count without the specified scaling and denominator.

questions.hint: Combine stillbirths and early neonatal deaths, and include stillbirths in the denominator.
questions.lesson: Perinatal mortality and maternal mortality use different events and denominator definitions.
questions.explanation: The numerator is 40 + 10 and the denominator is 9,960 + 40. This gives 5.00 per 1,000 total births. The maternal deaths belong to a separate indicator.

review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Update survival after right censoring.
questions.stem: Ten patients are initially unrecovered. Two recover on day 1. Two other patients stop being observed on day 2 while still unrecovered. One recovers on day 3. The rest are still observed. What is the Kaplan–Meier estimate of remaining unrecovered just after day 3?

options.feedback: That treats all five exits as events.
Three events divided by ten ignores the later risk set.
The two survival factors are 8/10 and 5/6.
There were six still at risk at the last event.
5/6 is the conditional day 3 factor alone.

questions.hint: Write the risk set just before each event time.
questions.lesson: Define the start of follow-up, event and censoring. A right-censored participant contributes observed time at risk. Kaplan–Meier multiplies conditional probabilities of remaining free of the specified event. Death before relapse prevents first relapse and enters its real-world cumulative incidence as a competing event. Log-rank compares curves using observed and expected event counts. A Cox hazard ratio describes relative instantaneous event rates. Its usual constant summary assumes proportional hazards.
questions.explanation: (1 − 2/10) × (1 − 1/6) = 2/3. The two censorings reduce the later risk set.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Choose an observed-world probability estimator.
questions.stem: An oncology team wants the probability that a first documented relapse occurs within one year of starting follow-up. A patient who dies relapse-free cannot subsequently relapse. Some are lost to follow-up alive and relapse-free. Which analysis best answers the question?

options.text: Censor deaths and report 1 minus Kaplan–Meier.
options.feedback: It can overestimate relapse probability by treating death as ordinary loss of observation.

options.text: Report the cause-specific relapse hazard at one year.
options.feedback: That is an instantaneous rate.

options.text: Report first relapse or death as one endpoint.
options.feedback: This gives the risk of a composite outcome.

options.text: Estimate relapse cumulative incidence with pre-relapse death as a competing event.
options.feedback: This accounts for the competing event that prevents a future first relapse.

options.text: Exclude everyone who dies before relapse at the start.
options.feedback: That conditions selection on a future outcome.

questions.hint: Identify which event prevents a future first relapse.
questions.lesson: Define the start of follow-up, event and censoring. A right-censored participant contributes observed time at risk. Kaplan–Meier multiplies conditional probabilities of remaining free of the specified event. Death before relapse prevents first relapse and enters its real-world cumulative incidence as a competing event. Log-rank compares curves using observed and expected event counts. A Cox hazard ratio describes relative instantaneous event rates. Its usual constant summary assumes proportional hazards.
questions.explanation: Use a cumulative incidence estimator for first relapse with death before relapse as a competing event. Handle loss of follow-up as right censoring under suitable assumptions.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Recognise a changing relative effect.
questions.stem: An intensive care trial shows higher early mortality with treatment, then lower later mortality. A Cox model gives HR 0.98 and scaled Schoenfeld residuals show a strong time trend. Which is the best next step?

options.text: Examine a time-varying effect and report absolute survival at prespecified times.
options.feedback: That represents the changing contrast and gives clinically interpretable comparisons.

options.text: Conclude that survival is equivalent.
options.feedback: A near-one summary does not establish equivalence.

options.text: Report 2% lower 90-day mortality risk.
options.feedback: A hazard ratio is an instantaneous contrast.

options.text: Ignore the residual plot because Cox regression is nonparametric.
options.feedback: The baseline hazard is unspecified, but the covariate ratio still has model assumptions.

options.text: Publish only a log-rank P value.
options.feedback: A single test result can hide opposing differences.

questions.hint: Ask whether a constant relative rate is appropriate.
questions.lesson: Define the start of follow-up, event and censoring. A right-censored participant contributes observed time at risk. Kaplan–Meier multiplies conditional probabilities of remaining free of the specified event. Death before relapse prevents first relapse and enters its real-world cumulative incidence as a competing event. Log-rank compares curves using observed and expected event counts. A Cox hazard ratio describes relative instantaneous event rates. Its usual constant summary assumes proportional hazards.
questions.explanation: If the relative effect changes, examine the time pattern and report absolute survival at relevant times. Restricted mean survival time over a prespecified horizon is another interpretable estimand.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Convert an odds ratio to risk at a stated baseline.
questions.stem: A severity-adjusted logistic model gives OR 0.50 for reattendance with a new respiratory protocol. At the same severity profile, what new-protocol risk corresponds to an old-protocol risk of 50%?

options.feedback: That halves probability rather than odds.
Old odds are 1. New odds are 0.5, giving risk 0.5/(1+0.5).
An OR of 0.50 changes the odds at this profile.
That doubles old odds.
That corresponds to odds of 3.

questions.hint: Convert baseline risk to odds before applying the ratio.
questions.lesson: Linear regression models a mean in the outcome's units, logistic regression models log odds for a binary outcome, and a Poisson model with a log exposure offset models a count rate. Adjust for selected covariates using the design and subject knowledge. Assess functional form, residuals, uncertainty and, for prediction, calibration beyond the development fit.
questions.explanation: Multiply the old odds 1 by 0.50, then divide the new odds by one plus those odds. The resulting risk is 1/3.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Model event rates with unequal exposure.
questions.stem: Clinics contribute different person-months and counts of unplanned visits. Which model directly estimates a visit rate ratio for clinic type?

options.text: Logistic regression on raw visit counts.
options.feedback: Visits are counts, and a person can make more than one.

options.text: Linear regression on raw visit counts.
options.feedback: Raw counts differ with the exposure time even at the same rate.

options.text: Poisson regression with an unlogged person-time offset.
options.feedback: Use the log exposure with the log link.

options.text: Poisson regression with log person-time as an estimated predictor.
options.feedback: A freely fitted exposure slope models a different relationship.

options.text: Poisson regression with log person-time as an offset.
options.feedback: This models expected count in proportion to exposure and exponentiates the clinic-type coefficient as a rate ratio.

questions.hint: At equal rates, double the time means double the expected count.
questions.lesson: Linear regression models a mean in the outcome's units, logistic regression models log odds for a binary outcome, and a Poisson model with a log exposure offset models a count rate. Adjust for selected covariates using the design and subject knowledge. Assess functional form, residuals, uncertainty and, for prediction, calibration beyond the development fit.
questions.explanation: With log expected count = log person-time plus the linear predictor, the clinic-type coefficient exponentiates to a rate ratio. Check dispersion and clustering when estimating its uncertainty.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Distinguish ranking from accurate risk predictions.
questions.stem: An anaesthesia complications model has AUC 0.85 at a new hospital. Among patients in groups with predicted risks of 20%, 50% and 80%, observed risks are 15%, 40% and 70% with large denominators. Which is the best interpretation?

options.text: AUC 0.85 establishes accurate risk for 85% of individuals.
options.feedback: AUC measures ranking of cases and non-cases.

options.text: The model underpredicts in these groups.
options.feedback: Observed risk is lower than predicted in each group.

options.text: The model discriminates fairly well and overpredicts in these groups.
options.feedback: Ranking and calibration measure different properties.

options.text: AUC above 0.80 makes calibration unnecessary.
options.feedback: A clinical decision threshold needs interpretable probabilities.

options.text: Drop the highest risk group to optimise the estimate.
options.feedback: That changes the target population and obscures performance.

questions.hint: Compare each observed risk with its matched prediction.
questions.lesson: Linear regression models a mean in the outcome's units, logistic regression models log odds for a binary outcome, and a Poisson model with a log exposure offset models a count rate. Adjust for selected covariates using the design and subject knowledge. Assess functional form, residuals, uncertainty and, for prediction, calibration beyond the development fit.
questions.explanation: High discrimination can coexist with overprediction. Assess calibration across the intended range with uncertainty and investigate transportability.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Compare individual differences with a tolerance.
questions.stem: A new paediatric monitor correlates 0.99 with the existing one. For new minus existing, mean bias is +2.5 units and estimated limits of agreement are +0.16 to +4.84. Differences above 3 units in either direction matter clinically. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Correlation establishes interchangeability.
options.feedback: Ranking can agree even when paired differences are large.

options.text: The estimated upper limit exceeds the tolerance. Assess uncertainty before deciding on replacement.
options.feedback: The point estimate exceeds +3 and the estimates have sampling uncertainty.

options.text: A mean bias below 3 implies all individual differences are acceptable.
options.feedback: Mean bias summarises the average, rather than individual spread.

options.text: The two limits are the confidence interval for mean bias.
options.feedback: Limits of agreement describe individual differences.

options.text: Subtract the mean bias and declare all future readings safe.
options.feedback: A correction may reduce systematic bias, but residual spread and validation still matter.

questions.hint: Compare the limit estimates with the prespecified range.
questions.lesson: Correlation measures association. Two devices can rank patients almost identically and still give differences large enough to change care. For paired quantitative measures, inspect differences against their means and compare the limits of agreement with a prespecified acceptable range. For two categorical raters report the agreement table and observed agreement alongside Cohen's kappa. For quantitative reliability specify the ICC design, single or average rating, and whether absolute agreement or consistency matters.
questions.explanation: The limit at +4.84 exceeds +3. Review its uncertainty and the clinical consequences. High correlation and an average difference below 3 are insufficient evidence for replacing the device.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Calculate Cohen's kappa from a table.
questions.stem: Two emergency clinicians classify 100 fictional records. Both mark 36 positive and both mark 52 negative. Clinician A alone marks 4 positive and clinician B alone marks 8 positive. What is unweighted Cohen's kappa, to two decimals?

options.feedback: This is the observed disagreement fraction.
This is approximately the marginal expected agreement.
This is the observed agreement.
This subtracts expected agreement from observed, but omits the scaling denominator.

questions.hint: Use both positive and negative marginals to calculate expected agreement.
questions.lesson: Correlation measures association. Two devices can rank patients almost identically and still give differences large enough to change care. For paired quantitative measures, inspect differences against their means and compare the limits of agreement with a prespecified acceptable range. For two categorical raters report the agreement table and observed agreement alongside Cohen's kappa. For quantitative reliability specify the ICC design, single or average rating, and whether absolute agreement or consistency matters.
questions.explanation: A's positive/negative fractions are 0.40/0.60 and B's 0.44/0.56. Their cross-products for matching categories sum to 0.512. Divide 0.88 − 0.512 by 1 − 0.512.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Choose a reliability estimate that matches single-reader use.
questions.stem: Every image in a reliability study is read by the same two clinicians, viewed as a sample from eligible readers. In practice one reader's numerical value will be used. Systematic differences between readers matter. Which ICC specification best fits this use?

options.text: Two-way consistency, average of two readers.
options.feedback: Both the definition and number of readings differ from the intended use.

options.text: One-way random-effects ICC for a single reading.
options.feedback: The same readers assess all images, allowing their effects to be separated in a two-way design.

options.text: Two-way random-reader absolute agreement, single reading.
options.feedback: It addresses generalising to eligible readers, one deployed reading and systematic differences.

options.text: Two-way absolute agreement for the average of two readings.
options.feedback: An average often has higher reliability than a single reading, but a single reading is used here.

options.text: Pearson correlation of the two readers' scores.
options.feedback: Correlation does not penalise a systematic shift.

questions.hint: Ask who reads each image, how many readings are used and whether absolute values matter.
questions.lesson: Correlation measures association. Two devices can rank patients almost identically and still give differences large enough to change care. For paired quantitative measures, inspect differences against their means and compare the limits of agreement with a prespecified acceptable range. For two categorical raters report the agreement table and observed agreement alongside Cohen's kappa. For quantitative reliability specify the ICC design, single or average rating, and whether absolute agreement or consistency matters.
questions.explanation: Use two-way random-reader absolute agreement for a single measurement under the stated design and assumptions. Report its form and interval alongside the clinical consequences of measurement differences.

review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Interpret equal proportions with unequal denominators.
questions.stem: An emergency department's stable baseline is 8% delayed reviews. One later month has 15 delays among 100 eligible encounters, another has 45 among 300. Using a simple 3 SD binomial p-chart with baseline fixed, which statement is correct?

options.text: Both breach because both exceed 8%.
options.feedback: The centre line is not a control limit.

options.text: Both must give the same signal because both equal 15%.
options.feedback: The denominator determines the width of the band.

options.text: The smaller month breaches first because its estimate is noisier.
options.feedback: Expected variation is greater at smaller n, so the limit is wider.

options.text: Only the 300-encounter month breaches the upper limit.
options.feedback: The two limits are about 16.1% and 12.7%.

options.text: No control limit can be calculated without a clinical target.
options.feedback: The limits use the baseline proportion and denominator.

questions.hint: Calculate 0.08 + 3√(0.08×0.92/n) in each month.
questions.lesson: An audit defines a standard, eligibility and a denominator, checks current care, acts on findings and remeasures. Quality improvement measures are followed in time order with a stable definition. A control chart estimates expected variation in a stable process. A p-chart models the proportion of eligible encounters with a binary outcome and its limits vary with denominator. Clinical targets, control limits and confidence intervals serve different purposes.
questions.explanation: At n=100 the limit is 16.1%, so 15% is within it. At n=300 it is 12.7%, so 15% breaches it. Verify the observation and investigate a potential special cause.

review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Choose a response to stable performance short of a standard.
questions.stem: For a year an ICU process has remained within its established control limits, with no chart-rule signals. The service’s target maximum adverse-event rate is below every observed rate. Which action fits this evidence?

options.text: Study and redesign the underlying process, then continue monitoring.
options.feedback: Stable process variation can coexist with performance below the standard.

options.text: Investigate each fluctuation as a separate staff error.
options.feedback: Ordinary variation need not have a separate assignable cause in each month.

options.text: Raise the target to the current centre and declare success.
options.feedback: The service target and process centre answer different questions.

options.text: Use the latest value as evidence of a sustained improvement.
options.feedback: A single point within the observed pattern does not show a sustained change.

options.text: Stop measuring because the process is statistically stable.
options.feedback: Stability says little about whether care meets a clinical standard.

questions.hint: Decide separately whether the process is stable and whether it meets the standard.
questions.lesson: An audit defines a standard, eligibility and a denominator, checks current care, acts on findings and remeasures. Quality improvement measures are followed in time order with a stable definition. A control chart estimates expected variation in a stable process. A p-chart models the proportion of eligible encounters with a binary outcome and its limits vary with denominator. Clinical targets, control limits and confidence intervals serve different purposes.
questions.explanation: A stable process can consistently perform poorly. Examine its underlying design, monitor for change after intervention and keep the clinical target distinct from expected process variation.

questions.objective: Use common weights to compare sites.
questions.stem: For an illustrative site comparison, low/high-frailty rates per 1,000 patient-days are 1 and 6 at A, and 2 and 8 at B. Crude rates are 4.75 at A and 3.2 at B. With a common 50:50 person-time mix, what are the directly standardised rates?

options.feedback: Those are the crude rates with each site's own mix.
Apply the same half weight to each stratum in each site.
Add the two stratum rates only after weighting them.
The weighted rates have been assigned to the opposite sites.
That compares the low-frailty stratum alone.

questions.hint: Apply the same weights to both sets of stratum rates.
questions.lesson: An audit defines a standard, eligibility and a denominator, checks current care, acts on findings and remeasures. Quality improvement measures are followed in time order with a stable definition. A control chart estimates expected variation in a stable process. A p-chart models the proportion of eligible encounters with a binary outcome and its limits vary with denominator. Clinical targets, control limits and confidence intervals serve different purposes.
questions.explanation: A is 0.5×1 + 0.5×6 = 3.5 and B is 0.5×2 + 0.5×8 = 5.0. The common mix reverses the crude comparison. Case-mix adjustment does not settle measurement comparability or uncertainty.

questions.objective: Calculate an absolute benefit.
questions.stem: A 90-day trial reports that 30 of 500 people allocated to a new treatment and 50 of 500 allocated to usual care had at least one admission. How many fewer people per 1,000 allocated to the new treatment had at least one admission by day 90, compared with usual care?

options.feedback: Twenty is the raw difference between groups of 500.
The absolute difference of 0.04 corresponds to 40 fewer people with at least one admission per 1,000.
Sixty per 1,000 is the treatment risk.
One hundred per 1,000 is the usual care risk.
40% is the relative reduction in the risk of having at least one admission. The question asks for the absolute difference per 1,000 people.

questions.hint: Calculate the two risks before subtracting.
questions.lesson: Report a common denominator and time.
questions.explanation: The absolute difference is 50/500 − 30/500 = 0.04. This estimates 40 fewer people with at least one admission per 1,000 allocated to the new treatment by day 90.

questions.objective: Calculate the number needed to harm.
questions.stem: Serious rash occurs in 15 of 500 treated patients and 5 of 500 usual-care patients by 90 days. What is the estimated number needed to harm for serious rash?

options.feedback: Ten is the raw excess count, not a number needed to harm.
Twenty is the excess per 1,000 patients.
This roughly inverts the treated risk alone.
Take the reciprocal of the 0.02 risk increase.
This inverts the usual-care risk alone.

questions.hint: Subtract the risks, not the raw counts.
questions.lesson: The number needed to harm refers to a particular outcome over a particular time.
questions.explanation: The extra risk is 15/500 − 5/500 = 0.02. Its reciprocal is 50 for one additional serious rash by 90 days.

questions.objective: Distinguish absolute and relative effects across settings.
questions.stem: Assume a treatment's 90-day admission risk ratio of 0.60 also applies in a clinic where untreated risk is 2.5%. What absolute benefit would this model predict?

options.text: 1.0 percentage point
options.feedback: Treated risk would be 0.60 × 2.5% = 1.5%.

options.text: 1.5 percentage points
options.feedback: This is the predicted treated risk expressed as a percentage, not the reduction.

options.text: 2.5 percentage points
options.feedback: This is the untreated risk.

options.text: 4.0 percentage points
options.feedback: A 4.0-point reduction would require a 10% untreated risk at this risk ratio. The untreated risk here is 2.5%.

options.text: 40 percentage points
options.feedback: This confuses a 40% relative reduction with an absolute difference.

questions.hint: What treated risk does the stated ratio imply?
questions.lesson: Absolute benefit depends on baseline risk if relative benefit is held constant.
questions.explanation: Under the stated assumption, the predicted treated risk is 1.5% and the absolute reduction is 1.0 percentage point. Transporting the risk ratio is itself an assumption.

questions.objective: Recognise interaction on the absolute scale.
questions.stem: A treatment halves event risk in both age strata. Untreated risks are 10% in younger people and 30% in older people. How do absolute benefits compare?

options.text: They are each 50 percentage points.
options.feedback: The ratio halves the stated baseline risk; it does not subtract 50 points.

options.text: They must be identical.
options.feedback: An identical ratio need not produce an identical risk difference.

options.text: 5 points younger, 15 points older.
options.feedback: Halving the two baseline risks prevents different numbers of events per 100.

options.text: 15 points younger, 5 points older.
options.feedback: The higher baseline risk has the larger absolute benefit here.

options.text: They cannot be calculated.
options.feedback: The baseline risks and the stratum-specific ratios suffice for these contrasts.

questions.hint: Halve each untreated risk and subtract.
questions.lesson: Effect modification depends on the scale.
questions.explanation: Risk moves from 10% to 5%, and from 30% to 15%. The absolute reduction is larger in the older group.

questions.objective: Distinguish confounders and mediators.
questions.stem: Baseline illness severity affects both treatment uptake and later admission. Treatment reduces symptoms at one week, and that change affects admission. Which adjustment set is most appropriate for the total treatment effect, assuming no other common causes and this causal structure?

options.text: One-week symptoms only.
options.feedback: Symptoms are downstream of the treatment and lie on a pathway to the outcome.

options.text: Neither variable.
options.feedback: Baseline severity opens a noncausal association between treatment and admission.

options.text: Both variables.
options.feedback: Adjusting for symptoms can block part of the total effect.

options.text: Baseline illness severity only.
options.feedback: This addresses the stated confounding without removing the effect through symptoms.

options.text: Only people who improve by one week.
options.feedback: Selecting on a post-treatment variable can bias the comparison.

questions.hint: Order the variables in time and ask which precedes treatment.
questions.lesson: Choose controls for the causal effect of interest.
questions.explanation: Baseline severity is a common cause; the subsequent symptoms are a mediator in the stated structure. Adjustment for the mediator does not in general estimate the total effect.

questions.objective: Identify a threat to comparing treatment strategies.
questions.stem: In one patient subgroup, nobody receives the new treatment. What limits an adjusted comparison for that subgroup using only this cohort?

options.text: There is no treatment overlap in that subgroup.
options.feedback: A data-based comparison needs observations under both strategies within the subgroup.

options.text: The problem disappears by choosing logistic regression.
options.feedback: A model can extrapolate, but this is not evidence under the unobserved strategy.

options.text: A larger sample with the same treatment rule guarantees overlap.
options.feedback: A rule that excludes treatment in this subgroup can persist at any sample size.

options.text: Only the confidence level needs changing.
options.feedback: Confidence levels do not supply missing treatment comparisons.

options.text: The subgroup proves the treatment is ineffective.
options.feedback: It provides no observed treated outcome.

questions.hint: Can we observe both strategies for these patients?
questions.lesson: Positivity is a condition for identification from observed comparisons.
questions.explanation: The data lack overlap in this subgroup. Change the question to a supported population or state and justify external information or extrapolation.

questions.objective: Distinguish the interval for a mean effect from an interval for a new setting.
questions.stem: A meta-analysis estimates a 2-day average reduction in recovery time. Its 95% confidence interval for the mean excludes zero, but its prediction interval includes no reduction and some prolongation. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Every setting should expect a shorter recovery.
options.feedback: A confidence interval for a mean does not describe every setting.

options.text: The study outcomes must have been measured incorrectly.
options.feedback: The pattern can arise from real heterogeneity.

options.text: The two results contradict each other.
options.feedback: They are intervals for different quantities.

options.text: The result rules out increased recovery time in a new setting.
options.feedback: The prediction interval allows such an effect.

options.text: The estimated average favours the intervention, but effects in comparable settings may differ.
options.feedback: The distinction matters when choosing whether to adopt the intervention.

questions.hint: Ask what each interval is intended to cover.
questions.lesson: A pooled effect is a summary of study evidence, not a guaranteed local effect.
questions.explanation: The mean-effect interval reflects uncertainty in the average. A prediction interval accounts for heterogeneity and allows no benefit or harm in a comparable setting under the model.

questions.objective: Interpret funnel plot asymmetry.
questions.stem: Small studies in a systematic review report larger benefits than larger studies. What can be concluded from this finding alone?

options.text: Selective publication is proven.
options.feedback: It is one possible explanation, not proven by the pattern.

options.text: Several explanations are possible, including selective reporting and genuine differences in populations.
options.feedback: The pattern prompts checks of study methods, setting and missing results.

options.text: The pooled effect is automatically unbiased with random effects.
options.feedback: Random effects do not correct biased studies or absent results.

options.text: All small studies must be excluded in every review.
options.feedback: Exclusion needs a principled, preferably prespecified reason.

options.text: The largest study is definitely correct.
options.feedback: Size does not guarantee good design or applicability.

questions.hint: Distinguish a signal from its cause.
questions.lesson: Different results in smaller studies call for investigation.
questions.explanation: Larger benefits reported in smaller studies have several possible explanations. Consider chance, genuine differences in populations or methods, and selective reporting or publication.

questions.objective: Assess the certainty of an effect estimate in a target population.
questions.stem: A review finds a precise benefit in young adults. The decision concerns frail older people with multiple conditions who were excluded from all studies. Which aspect is specifically threatened by this mismatch?

options.text: Indirectness
options.feedback: The included population differs from those to whom the result would apply.

options.text: Sampling imprecision in the pooled estimate
options.feedback: The interval can be narrow even when populations differ.

options.text: Inter-rater reliability
options.feedback: There is no stated measurement disagreement.

options.text: Publication bias
options.feedback: Differences in participants do not establish suppressed results.

options.text: Allocation concealment
options.feedback: How assignment was hidden is a separate study-level concern.

questions.hint: Ask who was studied and who will receive treatment.
questions.lesson: Certainty depends partly on how directly the studies answer your question.
questions.explanation: Even a precise estimate can be indirect for a different population. Assess the clinical reasons that the benefit or harm might change.

questions.objective: Calculate a population attributable fraction from a stated scenario.
questions.stem: A population has 300 annual cases. A defined intervention is expected to prevent 50 of them without other changes. What proportion of the current population cases would it prevent?

options.feedback: This might be a change in population risk if population size were known, not the proportion of current cases.
This is not the ratio of prevented to observed cases.
Fifty divided by 300 is one sixth.
The numerator is a count of 50 cases.
This is the fraction of cases expected to remain.

questions.hint: Use the total number of current cases as the denominator.
questions.lesson: Keep population risk and fraction of cases distinct.
questions.explanation: Under the assumptions the intervention would avert 50/300, or about 16.7% of current cases.

questions.objective: Translate a causal risk ratio into relative vaccine effectiveness.
questions.stem: With equal ascertainment and adequate follow-up, a fictional randomised vaccine trial estimates a risk ratio of 0.25 for symptomatic infection, vaccine versus placebo. What is vaccine efficacy on the relative risk-reduction scale?

options.feedback: The reciprocal risk ratio is 1/0.25 = 4. Vaccine efficacy instead uses (1 − 0.25) × 100% = 75%.
This is the vaccinated group's risk relative to placebo.
The reduction is not half here.
Relative risk reduction is one minus the risk ratio.
Some symptomatic infections remain in the vaccinated group.

questions.hint: Compare the ratio with a ratio of one.
questions.lesson: Name the endpoint and duration when reporting efficacy.
questions.explanation: The estimated efficacy against symptomatic infection is 1 − 0.25 = 75% over the trial follow-up. This does not imply 75 fewer cases per 100 vaccinated.

questions.objective: Calculate an incremental cost per QALY.
questions.stem: For a fictional programme the expected extra total cost is 50,000 currency units and the expected extra health gain is 2 QALYs against current care. What is the incremental cost per QALY?

options.feedback: Divide incremental costs by incremental QALYs.
This is the total incremental cost.
100,000 comes from multiplying 50,000 by 2. Incremental cost per QALY divides the extra cost by the extra QALYs.
This is the incremental health gain.

options.text: It cannot be computed without the total cost of each plan.
options.feedback: The differences suffice for this arithmetic.

questions.hint: What additional cost corresponds to one additional QALY?
questions.lesson: An incremental ratio compares two stated strategies.
questions.explanation: 50,000 / 2 = 25,000 currency units per additional QALY. Whether the programme represents value requires evidence and a decision framework.

questions.objective: Calculate the familywise error probability under independent true nulls.
questions.stem: Twenty independent tests all have true null hypotheses. Each rejects falsely with probability 0.05. What is the probability of at least one false rejection?

options.feedback: This is the probability for a single test.
This is close to the probability of no false rejections.
The probability should be calculated from the complement.
The complement of 0.95 to the 20th power is about 0.642.
The expected number of false rejections is one; that does not mean at least one is certain.

questions.hint: Calculate the probability all 20 avoid a false rejection.
questions.lesson: A familywise error rate concerns at least one error among a set of tests.
questions.explanation: Under independence the probability is 1 − 0.95^20 ≈ 64.2%. Under dependence this formula generally changes.

questions.objective: Calculate a worst-case risk difference with missing binary outcomes.
questions.stem: In a fictional trial with 100 patients per arm, 10 outcomes in each arm are unknown. Known event totals are 8 in treatment and 12 in control. What is the largest possible treatment-minus-control risk difference?

options.text: −14 percentage points
options.feedback: This is the smallest possible difference.

options.text: −4 percentage points
options.feedback: Equal numbers of events among missing participants in the two arms would leave the difference at −4 points.

options.text: 0 percentage points
options.feedback: The extremes allow an excess in treatment.

options.text: +4 percentage points
options.feedback: +4 reverses the difference for the known events. To maximise treatment minus control, assign an event to all ten missing treatment participants and to none of the missing controls. That gives +6 points.

options.text: +6 percentage points
options.feedback: The extreme is (8 + 10)/100 − 12/100.

questions.hint: Make treatment risk as high and control risk as low as possible.
questions.lesson: A worst-case bound does not require missing outcomes to be random.
questions.explanation: The maximum is 18% − 12% = 6 percentage points. This ignores sampling uncertainty: it is a bound for the observed trial cohort.

questions.objective: Recognise missing not at random.
questions.stem: Even after accounting for recorded baseline severity, patients with higher unrecorded outcome symptom scores are less likely to respond. Which missingness description fits the stated mechanism?

options.text: Missing not at random
options.feedback: Response still depends on the unobserved outcome after conditioning on measured variables.

options.text: Missing completely at random
options.feedback: Response is not independent of the data.

options.text: Missing at random given baseline severity
options.feedback: The stem specifies dependence on the unobserved outcome even at the same severity.

options.text: No missing-data problem after complete-case analysis
options.feedback: Dropping missing outcomes does not remove selection on the outcome.

options.text: Randomisation guarantees unbiased complete-case comparison
options.feedback: Allocation does not guarantee that observed outcomes are a representative subset.

questions.hint: What information predicts response after conditioning on measured variables?
questions.lesson: The missingness mechanism is an assumption, not determined by the observed data alone.
questions.explanation: The hypothetical mechanism depends on the missing outcome itself after accounting for observed covariates, so it is MNAR.

questions.objective: Identify controls from the population that produced the cases.
questions.stem: A clinic studies whether an exposure is associated with an acute condition using a case-control design. Cases are residents of its catchment who developed the condition during one year. Which criterion matters most for selecting controls?

options.text: They had no exposure of interest.
options.feedback: Selecting on exposure can distort the comparison.

options.text: Their age exactly equals the mean age of the cases.
options.feedback: Source population membership is central. Matching is optional and does not mean selecting the case-group mean.

options.text: They come from people who could have been identified as cases had they developed the condition that year.
options.feedback: Controls should reflect the relevant population and time at risk.

options.text: They are from a different region with no access to the clinic.
options.feedback: The region may have a different exposure distribution and different case ascertainment.

options.text: Their number equals the number of cases.
options.feedback: The number of controls concerns precision, not the fundamental selection criterion.

questions.hint: Ask where the cases came from before matching or counting controls.
questions.lesson: Controls provide a comparison of exposure in a specified source population.
questions.explanation: Controls should come from the source population that generated the cases under the study's eligibility and ascertainment rules.

questions.objective: Interpret an odds ratio without mistaking a case-control sample for a cohort.
questions.stem: A case-control study observes 40 exposed and 20 unexposed cases, and 20 exposed and 40 unexposed controls. Which quantity can be calculated directly as a population association estimate under appropriate sampling?

options.text: Population disease prevalence of 50%
options.feedback: The number of cases sampled was chosen by design.

options.text: Population risk difference of 33 percentage points
options.feedback: There are no population disease-risk denominators here.

options.text: Risk ratio of 2
options.feedback: The disease risks cannot be obtained from the selected counts.

options.text: Exposure odds ratio of 4
options.feedback: Divide 40/20 by 20/40.

options.text: Incidence rate of 60 per 120 person-years
options.feedback: The denominators are sampled people and do not measure person-time.

questions.hint: Compare the odds of exposure in cases with those in controls.
questions.lesson: Use effect measures that are identified by the sampling design.
questions.explanation: The odds ratio is (40 × 40)/(20 × 20) = 4. It is not automatically a risk ratio.

questions.objective: Identify a suitable qualitative contribution to a mixed-methods study.
questions.stem: Attendance records show low uptake of a service in certain locations. The team wants to understand why before changing delivery. Which next step best adds qualitative evidence?

options.text: Interview diverse eligible people and staff, examine recurring themes and integrate them with the uptake patterns.
options.feedback: This investigates reasons and adds to the quantitative description.

options.text: Treat non-attendance as proof of one common motive.
options.feedback: Records show an action, not the reasons for it.

options.text: Report each theme as its prevalence in the entire catchment.
options.feedback: A purposive qualitative sample does not usually support that inference.

options.text: Choose the most favourable explanation from an uptake chart.
options.feedback: The chart cannot establish participants' experiences.

options.text: Increase the significance threshold until the data explain the reasons.
options.feedback: A threshold change does not supply evidence about motives.

questions.hint: Which data would help you understand experiences?
questions.lesson: Use qualitative work to answer an explanatory question, then integrate the findings deliberately.
questions.explanation: Purposefully sample a range of perspectives, examine the narratives systematically and reconcile themes with the observed data.

questions.objective: Explain why single-test thresholds cannot be reused at every interim look.
questions.stem: A study plans to inspect accumulating outcome data each month and stop for efficacy at the first unadjusted P < 0.05. What is the main statistical concern with this rule?

options.text: The repeated looks can inflate the chance of a false positive.
options.feedback: A planned sequential design can control this probability while allowing monitoring.

options.text: Each look must be independent because a new month has passed.
options.feedback: The data commonly overlap across looks.

options.text: The null hypothesis automatically changes with each look.
options.feedback: The same hypothesis may be tested repeatedly.

options.text: A smaller P value always identifies the right treatment decision.
options.feedback: Results must account for monitoring and be interpreted alongside effects and harms.

options.text: An ethics review alone adjusts the significance level.
options.feedback: Ethical and statistical oversight are related but distinct.

questions.hint: How many opportunities are there to stop by chance?
questions.lesson: Specify how repeated looks and stopping rules affect inference before trial results are known.
questions.explanation: Repeated stopping opportunities can inflate the false-positive probability. Use a prespecified group-sequential or other suitable monitoring method that accounts for dependence.

questions.objective: Recognise re-identification risks when sharing analysis examples.
questions.stem: A trainee wants to send a dataset to a tutor. Names have been removed, but exact visit dates, rare diagnoses and free-text case notes remain. What is the best way to share a reproducible worked example with this tutor?

options.text: Send it because the name column has been removed.
options.feedback: Remaining variables can identify participants.

options.text: Send only the free-text notes.
options.feedback: Notes can contain direct or indirect identifiers.

options.text: Replace the names with participant IDs and email the file.
options.feedback: Pseudonymisation does not by itself authorise disclosure.

options.text: Use synthetic data that reproduce the analysis structure, and keep protected data within authorised systems.
options.feedback: This lets the tutor check methods while protecting participants.

options.text: Convert the worksheet to an image before sending.
options.feedback: The medium does not remove identifying content.

questions.hint: Can you reproduce the method without sharing an actual row?
questions.lesson: Share code, definitions and synthetic examples when real participant data are not authorised for the recipient.
questions.explanation: Exact dates, uncommon diagnoses and free text can identify people. Synthetic data can illustrate the method without disclosing those records.

questions.objective: Distinguish prespecified and exploratory findings.
questions.stem: The prespecified comparison for the registered primary outcome did not meet the trial’s significance threshold. After seeing the results, investigators found a favourable subgroup and want to call that comparison the prespecified primary finding. What is the best response?

options.text: Redefine the primary analysis after seeing the subgroup result.
options.feedback: This conceals the selection process.

options.text: Report only the subgroup because it has the smallest P value.
options.feedback: Selective reporting distorts the evidence.

options.text: Report the registered outcome, disclose the exploratory subgroup search and seek independent confirmation.
options.feedback: Readers can distinguish planned evidence from a hypothesis generated by the data.

options.text: Declare the subgroup result false without further investigation.
options.feedback: An exploratory result can suggest a useful hypothesis.

options.text: Report that subgroup and overall effects are different without an interaction comparison.
options.feedback: A significant result in one subgroup and a nonsignificant result elsewhere do not establish interaction. Compare effect estimates directly with an appropriate interaction test.

questions.hint: Separate analyses agreed before seeing data from those prompted by the data.
questions.lesson: A clear record of decisions allows readers to judge the evidence.
questions.explanation: Keep the original outcome visible, label the analysis exploratory, account for the wider search and do not present the subgroup as confirmatory.

questions.objective: Use a DAG to choose adjustment for a total treatment effect.
questions.stem: For a fictional treatment T and later admission Y, the assumed arrows are A → T, A → Y, T → Y, T → M, M → Y, T → F, U → F and U → Y. A is age, M is early improvement, F is follow-up attendance and U is access to care. Which approach estimates the total treatment effect under this graph, given complete outcome measurement, overlap and consistency?

options.text: Adjust for age and early improvement.
options.feedback: Early improvement mediates part of the effect that the total-effect question includes.

options.text: Adjust for age alone.
options.feedback: Age blocks the backdoor path. Leaving M and F unconditioned preserves mediation and avoids opening the collider path.

options.text: Adjust for age and restrict to follow-up attendees.
options.feedback: Conditioning on attendance opens T → F ← U → Y.

options.text: Control only for access to care.
options.feedback: Access does not close T ← A → Y.

options.text: Use the unadjusted contrast.
options.feedback: Age affects both treatment and admission under the stated assumptions.

questions.hint: Trace the arrows entering T, then check where two arrows enter the same node.
questions.lesson: A DAG helps distinguish a confounder from a mediator and a collider.
questions.explanation: Age is the stated common cause of treatment and outcome. Adjustment for age closes the backdoor path. Conditioning on improvement removes a mediated pathway, and conditioning on attendance opens a path through access to care.

questions.objective: Read an individual line, pooled diamond and prediction interval on a forest plot.
questions.stem: A forest plot shows days to recovery, intervention minus usual care. One study's line spans −2.96 to +0.96 days. The pooled diamond spans −3.96 to −0.04 days. The separate prediction interval spans −5.93 to +1.93 days. Which reading is best?

options.text: The diamond shows that every study found a shorter recovery time.
options.feedback: The diamond represents the pooled estimate and its interval. Read individual rows separately.

options.text: The prediction interval estimates uncertainty about the average effect.
options.feedback: The diamond represents this uncertainty. The prediction interval includes variation in true effects across settings.

options.text: The individual study's confidence interval shows an effect of exactly zero.
options.feedback: The interval includes zero and both directions. It does not establish that the true effect is zero.

options.text: The pooled interval favours shorter recovery on average, while a comparable new setting could see a longer recovery time.
options.feedback: The diamond is below zero, while the prediction interval extends above zero.

options.text: The upper edge of the diamond rules out effects larger than zero in any comparable setting.
options.feedback: A confidence interval for the average does not bound the plausible true effect in each setting.

questions.hint: Zero represents no difference in recovery time. Identify which quantity each interval describes.
questions.lesson: The individual interval, pooled confidence interval and prediction interval answer different questions.
questions.explanation: The study line includes both shorter and longer recovery. The pooled confidence interval covers average effects below zero. The prediction interval includes zero and longer recovery times, conditional on the model.

questions.objective: Choose a mean comparison under heteroscedasticity.
questions.stem: Three independent groups of adults complete different fictional rehabilitation programmes. Each person gives one continuous score. Each group's distribution is roughly symmetric, the sample sizes and variances differ, and the planned question concerns any difference in population means. Which overall method fits the question?

options.text: A paired t test
options.feedback: This design has neither pairs nor a comparison limited to two means.

options.text: Ordinary ANOVA with a common variance
options.feedback: The common-variance model conflicts with the stated unequal variances.

options.text: Welch one-way ANOVA
options.feedback: It targets equality of independent group means without pooling within-group variance.

options.text: Friedman test
options.feedback: This requires related observations arranged in blocks.

options.text: Kruskal–Wallis rank test
options.feedback: It compares groups on the rank scale and does not directly target equality of arithmetic means.

questions.hint: Hold the target quantity fixed when deciding how to handle unequal variances.
questions.lesson: Welch's method retains the means as its target while allowing unequal group variances.
questions.explanation: The three groups are independent and the estimand concerns means. Welch one-way ANOVA addresses that global comparison with separate variance estimates and approximate degrees of freedom.
