questions.objective: Interpret a global F test and follow-up intervals.
questions.stem: An ordinary ANOVA comparing mean scores across three training formats gives P = 0.002. The investigators also report a 95% Tukey simultaneous confidence interval of −0.4 to +3.4 points for written training minus usual training. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: Every pair of population means differs.
options.feedback: The overall test cannot identify specific pairs.

options.text: The probability the written and usual means are equal is 0.002.
options.feedback: The overall P value is not a posterior probability and is not specific to this pair.

options.text: Written training improves the mean by exactly 1.5 points.
options.feedback: The interval midpoint is a point estimate with appreciable uncertainty.

options.text: The overall test gives evidence against all means being equal. The simultaneous comparison does not establish a written-versus-usual difference.
options.feedback: The small global P value and a pairwise interval that includes zero can coexist.

options.text: Written and usual training have been shown equivalent.
options.feedback: A confidence interval crossing zero does not establish equivalence. An equivalence claim requires justified margins and the appropriate analysis.

questions.hint: Separate the global null from the specific contrast and inspect its interval.
questions.lesson: An omnibus result can support an overall difference even when a chosen contrast is uncertain.
questions.explanation: The data provide evidence against equality of all three means. The simultaneous interval for written versus usual includes zero, so that pair's difference is not established by this analysis.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Recognise a continuous-outcome comparison with a baseline covariate.
questions.stem: A four-arm randomised study measures the same symptom score at baseline and 12 weeks. The protocol prespecifies a comparison of mean 12-week score adjusting for baseline score, using one common baseline slope for all arms. Which model has that structure?

options.text: ANCOVA with 12-week score as outcome, treatment as a factor and baseline score as a covariate
options.feedback: This fits a baseline-adjusted comparison conditional on the proposed common slope.

options.text: One-way ANOVA with 12-week score and treatment only
options.feedback: This compares groups without the prespecified baseline adjustment.

options.text: MANOVA jointly analysing baseline and 12-week scores as two responses
options.feedback: Two responses do not specify the requested baseline covariate model.

options.text: Kruskal–Wallis test of baseline scores
options.feedback: This neither models the 12-week outcome nor estimates the requested adjusted mean contrasts.

options.text: Friedman test treating treatment arms as repeated measurements on each participant
options.feedback: Each participant received one arm. Baseline and follow-up do not make the arms repeated conditions.

questions.hint: Ask which measurement is the outcome and which is the adjustment variable.
questions.lesson: A baseline covariate and a follow-up outcome play different roles in a regression model.
questions.explanation: Use ANCOVA with treatment indicators and a baseline covariate, then report prespecified adjusted contrasts and their intervals. Check whether the common-slope model is plausible.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Select a global rank comparison for several matched conditions.
questions.stem: Each of 18 participants rates the comfort of three fictional devices on a five-level ordered scale. Device order is randomised for each participant, every rating is observed, and a global comparison using within-person ranks is planned. Which test fits?

options.text: Kruskal–Wallis
options.feedback: This pools ranks across independent groups, whereas the device scores are matched by participant.

options.text: Cochran Q
options.feedback: It compares matched binary responses. The comfort scale has ordered categories beyond two levels.

options.text: Welch one-way ANOVA
options.feedback: This compares independent group means and does not use the ranking within each participant.

options.text: Friedman test
options.feedback: Rank the three scores within each participant and compare the conditions across the complete independent blocks.

options.text: Wilcoxon signed-rank test for one pair
options.feedback: A single comparison of two related conditions does not address the global three-condition question.

questions.hint: Identify where the ranking needs to happen and how many conditions are compared.
questions.lesson: Friedman is a global within-block rank comparison for repeated ordered responses.
questions.explanation: A complete row is one participant. Rank the device scores inside each row and compare their rank patterns over all participants.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Recognise the covariance assumption of an uncorrected F test.
questions.stem: The same adults complete each of three measurement conditions. Analysts propose the usual uncorrected univariate repeated-measures ANOVA F test. Which statement describes sphericity?

options.text: The condition means are equal.
options.feedback: That is the global mean null hypothesis, not the covariance assumption.

options.text: The population variances of all pairwise within-person differences are equal.
options.feedback: This is sphericity for a single within-person factor.

options.text: Each participant's repeated observations are independent.
options.feedback: A repeated design allows dependence within the same person.

options.text: The three marginal variances alone are equal.
options.feedback: Univariate marginal variances do not determine the variances of the differences, which also depend on covariance.

options.text: The observed ranks have no ties.
options.feedback: Ties affect rank calculations. Sphericity concerns variances of contrasts in the mean model.

questions.hint: Think about what varies when the same person's measurements are subtracted.
questions.lesson: Sphericity concerns within-participant differences, which depend on variances and covariances.
questions.explanation: For three conditions it requires equal population variances of A−B, A−C and B−C. A valid correction or a model with an appropriate covariance structure may be needed when it is untenable.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Choose a model that addresses trajectories with incomplete follow-up.
questions.stem: In a fictional two-arm trial, symptom scores are scheduled at baseline, 1 month, 3 months and 6 months. Some follow-ups are missed. The primary question is whether mean trajectories differ by arm. Which strategy most directly addresses this target?

options.text: Compare the groups separately at each observed visit using unadjusted independent tests.
options.feedback: Separate tests do not estimate the planned trajectory interaction and need a multiplicity plan.

options.text: Replace every missing score with zero, then analyse the independent rows.
options.feedback: Zero is an assumption about an unobserved outcome and repeated rows for each person are dependent.

options.text: Test change over time separately in each arm and infer a treatment difference if only one is significant.
options.feedback: A difference in statistical significance does not show a difference between arms. Estimate the arm-by-visit contrast directly.

options.text: Compare each person's last recorded score regardless of visit date.
options.feedback: Last observed values can represent different times and a changed target population.

options.text: Use a suitable longitudinal model with arm, visit and their interaction, accounting for within-person correlation and missingness assumptions.
options.feedback: It addresses mean trajectories and makes both the dependency and missing-data assumptions explicit.

questions.hint: Choose a method that represents treatment, time and observations from the same person together.
questions.lesson: A trajectory comparison is a treatment-by-time question, with a plan for within-person dependence and incomplete data.
questions.explanation: A suitable longitudinal model can use observed repeated outcomes on their intended schedule and estimate treatment-by-visit contrasts. Check the chosen covariance and missingness assumptions and consider sensitivity analyses.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Estimate a proportion with unequal sampling fractions.
questions.stem: A fictional city has 800 eligible people in one stratum and 200 in another. Independent random samples of 100 from each yield 15 and 45 people with the outcome. What is the population-weighted proportion estimate?

options.feedback: This is only the contribution from the larger stratum.
Weight 15% and 45% by the population shares 0.8 and 0.2.
This uses the equal sample sizes as weights.
This is only the estimate in the smaller stratum.
This sums the stratum estimates without weighting.

questions.hint: Use population shares, then add the two contributions.
questions.lesson: Known population shares combine the stratum estimates.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Identify the source of information for survey variance.
questions.stem: In a stratified survey, each stratum draws a simple random sample of clinics without replacement. Each clinic has the same number of eligible people and all people in sampled clinics respond. Which approach estimates the standard error of the overall proportion?

options.text: Calculate an unweighted binomial standard error using all people
options.feedback: That treats people as the independent sampling units.

options.text: Pool clinic proportions and use one overall clinic sampling fraction.
options.feedback: This ignores each stratum’s sampling fraction and its squared weight in the variance of the combined estimate.

options.text: Weight observations and then assume they are independently sampled
options.feedback: Correct point-estimate weights do not make within-clinic selections independent.

options.text: Use variation among sampled clinic proportions within strata and apply the finite population correction
options.feedback: Clinics were sampled separately within each stratum. Combine stratum variances with squared population shares.

options.text: Set the standard error to zero because all selected people responded
options.feedback: Complete response removes non-response here. There is still uncertainty from selecting a subset of clinics.

questions.hint: Identify the units randomly selected by the survey.
questions.lesson: A probability sample of clinics can estimate sampling variability from sampled clinics within each stratum.
questions.explanation: Use the sampled clinic proportions within strata, incorporate sampling fractions and then combine the independent stratum variances.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Combine model terms at a given post-intervention time.
questions.stem: A segmented regression estimates an immediate change of −4 incidents per 1,000 visits and a slope change of −1.2 per 1,000 visits per month. Time since intervention is coded zero at the first post-intervention observation. What is the fitted contrast with continuing the baseline trend four months after that observation?

options.text: −8.8 per 1,000 visits
options.feedback: Add the immediate change and four months of slope change.

options.text: −4.8 per 1,000 visits
options.feedback: This omits the immediate change.

options.text: −4.0 per 1,000 visits
options.feedback: This is the contrast at the start of the post-intervention period.

options.text: −1.2 per 1,000 visits
options.feedback: This is the slope change per month rather than the contrast after four months.

options.text: +0.8 per 1,000 visits
options.feedback: This reverses the direction of the slope change.

questions.hint: At the first post-intervention observation, time since intervention is zero.
questions.lesson: The contrast combines level change and elapsed time times slope change.
questions.explanation: The contrast is −4 + 4 × (−1.2) = −8.8 per 1,000 visits.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Use denominators when interpreting reported changes over time.
questions.stem: A clinic recorded 10 incidents in 1,000 visits in one month and 20 incidents in 3,000 visits in another. Assume the recording method and coverage stayed the same. What can you say about the observed incidents per visit?

options.text: They doubled
options.feedback: Only the incident count doubled.

options.text: They tripled
options.feedback: The visit denominator tripled.

options.text: They stayed constant
options.feedback: The numerator and denominator changed by different factors.

options.text: They fell from 10 to about 6.7 per 1,000 visits
options.feedback: Calculate the count divided by visits in each month and multiply by 1,000.

options.text: They cannot be calculated without each person's follow-up time
options.feedback: The requested denominator is the number of visits, which is supplied.

questions.hint: Divide each incident count by its own visit total.
questions.lesson: A larger count can accompany a lower rate.
questions.explanation: The observed rates are 10/1,000 and 20/3,000. This comparison alone cannot attribute the change to an intervention.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Choose a measure appropriate for geographic comparison.
questions.stem: Two districts have the same surveillance coverage and age mix. District A has 30 new diagnoses among 3,000 people at risk. District B has 80 among 20,000. Which interpretation is correct for this period?

options.text: District B has the higher observed risk because 80 is larger than 30
options.feedback: This compares counts only.

options.text: Both risks are equal because they use the same case definition
options.feedback: Comparable case definitions do not make the risks equal.

options.text: District A has the higher observed risk, although District B has more diagnoses
options.feedback: A has 10 per 1,000 and B has 4 per 1,000.

options.text: Neither observed risk can be calculated until every district has the same number of residents
options.feedback: Different denominator sizes can be compared using proportions.

options.text: There is proof of a causal effect of living in District A
options.feedback: These summaries cannot rule out other explanations for the geographic difference.

questions.hint: Divide each count by its own district denominator.
questions.lesson: The rate or risk can rank places differently from a count.
questions.explanation: The observed proportion is 1% in A and 0.4% in B. The case count is larger in B.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Interpret a high rate based on sparse data.
questions.stem: A small area has one case among 100 residents at risk. A larger area has 100 cases among 20,000. The mapping system applies the same case definition and period in each. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Conclude the smaller area has twice the underlying risk
options.feedback: The observed estimates are in a 2:1 ratio, but the small area's rate is uncertain.

options.text: Display the smaller area's value as zero
options.feedback: A sparse or suppressed result is distinct from zero.

options.text: Investigate only if the small area has 100 cases
options.feedback: A single count threshold cannot decide whether a pattern warrants investigation.

options.text: Use only raw counts to compare risk
options.feedback: Raw counts reflect population size as well as disease frequency.

options.text: Examine uncertainty and detection before interpreting the difference
options.feedback: One additional case would double the smaller area's rate under the fixed denominator. Ascertainment can also differ.

questions.hint: Consider how moving one case affects each estimate.
questions.lesson: Sparse counts can change a rank even if the population at risk is well measured.
questions.explanation: The rates are 10 and 5 per 1,000. The former rests on one event, so seek comparable ascertainment and display or otherwise address uncertainty.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Use the comparator to calculate an incremental ratio.
questions.stem: After discounting, a fictional new programme costs £2,400 and yields 1.60 QALYs per person. Current care costs £2,000 and yields 1.55 QALYs over the same horizon. What is the incremental cost per additional QALY?

options.feedback: This divides the £400 increment by the new programme's total QALYs.
This is the incremental cost per person.
This divides the new programme's total cost by its total QALYs.
Divide the £400 difference in cost by the 0.05 difference in QALYs.
This divides the new programme's total cost by the incremental QALYs.

questions.hint: Compute differences in both columns before dividing.
questions.lesson: Incremental comparisons use differences in both costs and outcomes.
questions.explanation: The increment is (£2,400 − £2,000)/(1.60 − 1.55) = £8,000 per additional QALY.

review.reviewer: Codex review; Iain Buchan release approval
review.notes: Answer key, distractors and feedback independently checked.

questions.objective: Identify how a broader perspective changes the analysis.
questions.stem: A fictional programme reduces unpaid family care, but its original evaluation included only the provider's costs. What would address this limitation if a broader perspective is requested?

options.text: Include a stated valuation of changes in unpaid care, and vary that assumption in sensitivity analysis
options.feedback: A broader perspective can count the value of unpaid care. State how it is measured and valued, and check uncertainty.

options.text: Use a different discount rate without adding unpaid care to the resource inventory.
options.feedback: Discounting changes the value assigned to resources over time. It does not account for omitted unpaid care.

options.text: Treat the time as zero cost because no invoice was issued
options.feedback: Unpaid time can have an opportunity cost even without a payment.

options.text: Compare the intervention with no care even though current care is available
options.feedback: A realistic alternative is still needed.

options.text: Assume the programme saves money because care time falls
options.feedback: Other costs can offset the value of the reduction. Estimate the costs before concluding.

questions.hint: Ask which resources the requested perspective counts.
questions.lesson: Perspective determines which resource consequences enter the evaluation.
questions.explanation: Measure the change in unpaid care with a clear valuation method and show how different assumptions affect the conclusion.
